lessons.title: Context windows, caching and long documents
lessons.summary: Context is a finite, costly resource. Budget it, order it well, and cache what repeats.

sections.heading: Context is a budget
sections.body:
Everything counts: system prompt, tool definitions, CLAUDE.md, history, tool results, documents. Anthropic describes context as a finite **attention budget**: recall degrades as the window fills ("context rot"), so a detail buried among many irrelevant tokens is easier to miss. The goal is the smallest set of high-signal tokens that gets the job done.

Strategies:

- **Retrieve, don't dump.** Fetch the relevant chunks (search or retrieval tools) rather than pasting entire corpora.
- **Just-in-time retrieval.** Keep lightweight references (file paths, queries, ids) in context and load the data with tools when it is needed. A hybrid works well: a small amount up front (for example CLAUDE.md), the rest explored on demand.
- **Trim tool outputs.** Return the fields that matter, paginate and filter.
- **Isolate.** Send exploratory work to subagents that return condensed summaries.
- **Compact.** Summarize older turns while preserving decisions, open tasks and key facts. Clearing old tool results is the lightest-touch form.

sections.heading: Long-document prompting
sections.body:
- Put **long documents at the top** of the prompt and the **question or instructions at the end**. Anthropic reports this can improve response quality by up to 30% on long, multi-document inputs.
- Wrap each document in tags with metadata, e.g. `<document><source>...</source><document_content>...</document_content></document>`.
- Ask Claude to **extract relevant quotes first**, then answer from them. This grounds the answer and gives provenance.
- Use the **citations** capability where available to tie claims to source passages.

sections.heading: Prompt caching
sections.body:
- Mark the end of a stable prefix with `cache_control: {"type": "ephemeral"}`. Later requests that share **exactly the same prefix** read it from cache: much cheaper input and lower latency.
- The cache is **prefix-based** in order: `tools`, then `system`, then `messages`. Put stable content first (tools, system prompt, big documents) and variable content last. Place the breakpoint on the last block that stays identical, never on a block that contains a timestamp or per-user text.
- You can set **up to 4 breakpoints**; automatic (top-level) caching uses one of those slots. Each breakpoint only looks back a limited number of blocks for an earlier match, so long conversations need breakpoints placed deliberately.
- **Lifetime:** 5 minutes by default, refreshed every time the entry is read. A 1-hour TTL is available for traffic with longer gaps (for example batch jobs). Writes cost more than normal input (more for the 1-hour TTL); reads cost a small fraction of normal input.
- **Minimum length:** prefixes below the model's minimum cacheable length are simply not cached. No error is returned; you only see it in the usage fields.
- **What invalidates what:** changing tool definitions invalidates everything; changing `tool_choice`, images or thinking parameters invalidates the cached messages but not tools and system.
- **Verify** with `cache_creation_input_tokens` (written) and `cache_read_input_tokens` (hit).
- Best for: agents resending long system prompts and tool lists every turn, chat over a large document, many-shot example libraries.

keyPoints: Context is a finite attention budget: irrelevant tokens cost money and degrade recall.
Prefer just-in-time retrieval: references in context, data loaded by tools on demand.
Put long documents first and the question last, with each document in tags.
Extract quotes first to ground answers.
Prompt caching is prefix-based (tools, system, messages): stable content first, breakpoint, variable content after.
Up to 4 breakpoints; 5-minute default TTL refreshed on use, 1-hour option; short prefixes silently don't cache.

gotchas.trap: Put the timestamp at the top of the system prompt and cache it.
gotchas.correct: Keep variable content after the cached prefix, or the cache never hits.

gotchas.trap: Paste the full 400-page manual into every request.
gotchas.correct: Retrieve relevant sections, or cache the manual if it's reused across many requests.

gotchas.trap: Edit a tool description per request and expect the system prompt to stay cached.
gotchas.correct: Tools sit at the start of the prefix; changing them invalidates the whole cache.

gotchas.trap: A tiny prompt with cache_control returns no error, so it must be cached.
gotchas.correct: Below the minimum cacheable length nothing is cached; check cache_creation_input_tokens.

lessons.title: Reliability: memory, provenance, review, retries and evals
lessons.summary: Production agents must survive long tasks, flaky dependencies and their own mistakes.

sections.heading: Long-running work
sections.body:
- **Structured notes / memory files:** persist plans, progress and findings to files (for example `NOTES.md`, `PLAN.md`, `progress.json`, a memory tool) so work survives compaction or a fresh context window.
- **Checkpoint and resume:** store message history and session ids. Design tasks to be resumable and idempotent.
- **Persistent constraints:** a rule stated once early in a long session can be diluted by later context or summarized away by compaction. Keep critical constraints in always-loaded places (system prompt, CLAUDE.md) or enforce them in code, rather than in turn 3 of 200. In Claude Code the project-root CLAUDE.md is re-read after `/compact`; a rule that only lived in an early chat message can be summarized away.

sections.heading: Provenance and verification
sections.body:
- Require **sources** for factual claims (URLs, doc ids, file:line, quotes), especially in research and extraction. Quotes can be checked deterministically against the source text.
- **Independent review:** run the review in a separate instance or subagent with a fresh context, the original requirements and a rubric, rather than asking the generating session to check itself (the evaluator-optimizer pattern uses a separate evaluator). This is a design judgment rather than a documented benchmark: a fresh context is not anchored on the author's reasoning. Add deterministic checks (tests, schema validation, link checking) wherever possible.
- Allow "I don't know". Explicitly permitting uncertainty reduces hallucination.

sections.heading: Operational reliability
sections.body:
- **Know the errors:** 429 `rate_limit_error`, 500 `api_error`, 504 `timeout_error`, 529 `overloaded_error` (load across all users). These are transient: retry with **exponential backoff and jitter**, honour `retry-after`, and cap attempts. 400/401/403/404 are not fixed by retrying.
- **The official SDKs already retry** connection errors, 429 and 5xx (twice by default, with backoff, honouring `retry-after`). Tune `max_retries` rather than wrapping another unbounded loop around them.
- **Spend-cap 429:** a 429 caused by a spend limit has no `retry-after` and keeps failing. Stop, alert and surface it; backoff will not help.
- **Timeouts and streaming:** use streaming (or batches) for very long requests; set sensible client timeouts and `max_tokens`. Ramp traffic gradually, because sudden spikes can also be rate-limited.
- **Fallbacks:** after capped retries, degrade gracefully: a fallback model, a queued job, or a clear message to the user. Log the `request-id` header for support.
- **Message Batches API** for large, non-urgent workloads: asynchronous, about half the cost, most batches finish within 1 hour and they expire after 24 hours. Only succeeded requests are billed. Results can come back in any order, so match them by `custom_id`; handle `errored` and `expired` results by resubmitting.
- **Model routing:** smaller, faster models for simple steps, larger models for hard reasoning.
- **Evals:** a representative test set with clear success criteria (exact match, code-graded checks, LLM-as-judge with a rubric, human review), run on every prompt or model change. Monitor in production too.

keyPoints: Persist plans and progress in structured notes outside the context window.
Require provenance, and use independent instances plus deterministic checks for review.
Retry 429/529/5xx with exponential backoff and jitter, honouring retry-after; a spend-cap 429 needs a human, not retries.
The SDKs retry automatically; configure max_retries instead of stacking loops.
Use the Batches API for large asynchronous jobs at lower cost, matching results by custom_id.
Evals gate every prompt or model change.

gotchas.trap: Ask the agent at the end of a long session: "double-check your work".
gotchas.correct: Use a fresh, independent reviewer plus deterministic checks.

gotchas.trap: Retry immediately in a tight loop on 529.
gotchas.correct: Use exponential backoff with jitter and capped attempts.

gotchas.trap: Wrap the SDK call in your own 10-attempt retry loop.
gotchas.correct: The SDK already retries; stacked loops multiply attempts. Tune max_retries and add a fallback.

gotchas.trap: Assume batch results come back in submission order.
gotchas.correct: Match every result to its request by custom_id.

lessons.title: Long-horizon context engineering
lessons.summary: How agents keep working for hours: just-in-time retrieval, compaction, structured notes and sub-agent isolation.

sections.heading: Just-in-time retrieval
sections.body:
Instead of loading everything up front, the agent holds **lightweight references** (file paths, URLs, saved queries, record ids) and uses tools to pull in only what the current step needs. Claude Code works this way: CLAUDE.md loads at start, and the codebase is explored with search and read tools on demand.

- Pre-loading is faster per step but wastes budget on irrelevant material and goes stale.
- Pure exploration is slower but keeps the context focused.
- A **hybrid** (a small, stable briefing up front plus on-demand retrieval) is usually the right default.

sections.heading: Compaction and clearing
sections.body:
When a session nears the window limit, **compaction** summarizes the conversation and restarts from the summary. A good summary keeps decisions and their rationale, important facts, unresolved bugs, and current state and next steps; it drops raw tool output.

- **Clearing old tool results** is the lightest-touch option: once a large result has been used, it rarely needs to stay verbatim.
- In Claude Code, `/compact` triggers it manually, auto-compaction triggers it at a threshold, and a `PreCompact` hook can save state first. The Agent SDK compacts automatically and emits a `compact_boundary` message.
- The API also offers server-side compaction and context editing (beta) for your own agents.
- Rules that must survive belong in CLAUDE.md or the system prompt, which are re-supplied, not in an early chat turn.

sections.heading: Structured notes and sub-agents
sections.body:
- **Structured note-taking:** the agent writes progress to a file such as `NOTES.md` or a to-do list and reads it back after a reset. This gives persistent memory with almost no context overhead.
- **Sub-agent isolation:** a sub-agent starts with a fresh context, can spend many tokens exploring, and returns only a condensed summary (often around 1,000 to 2,000 tokens). The parent never sees the sub-agent's history, so the summary must carry what the parent needs, including sources.
- Choose by task shape: compaction for long back-and-forth, notes for iterative milestones, sub-agents for parallel or exploratory research.

keyPoints: Hold references, fetch data with tools when needed (just-in-time retrieval).
Compaction summarizes and restarts; clearing old tool results is the lightest touch.
Structured notes files survive context resets cheaply.
Sub-agents explore in isolation and return condensed summaries.
Persistent rules go in CLAUDE.md or the system prompt, not early chat turns.

gotchas.trap: Load the whole repository into the first message so the agent "knows everything".
gotchas.correct: Give it a short briefing and tools to search and read files on demand.

gotchas.trap: Have a sub-agent return its full transcript to the parent.
gotchas.correct: Return a condensed, sourced summary; isolation is the point.

lessons.lab: Run a long Claude Code task twice: once with no notes file, once instructing the agent to maintain NOTES.md. Force a /compact midway and compare how well each run resumes. Add a PreCompact hook that copies the current plan to disk.

flashcards.front: Which field drives the agent loop?
flashcards.back: stop_reason. Continue on "tool_use", resend on "pause_turn", and treat "end_turn" as the model finishing its turn. Handle the rest explicitly.

flashcards.front: What does stop_reason "max_tokens" mean?
flashcards.back: Output was truncated at your max_tokens limit. It's incomplete: raise the limit or continue, and don't parse it as final.

flashcards.front: Role of max_turns / iteration caps in an agent?
flashcards.back: A safety net against runaway loops, not the completion signal. Hitting it is an abnormal outcome to log or escalate.

flashcards.front: Why is checking reply text for "done" an anti-pattern?
flashcards.back: It's fragile: the model may say it mid-task or never say it. Use the structured stop_reason.

flashcards.front: Is the Messages API stateful?
flashcards.back: No. The client sends the full conversation history (plus system and tools) on every request.

flashcards.front: Workflow vs agent?
flashcards.back: Workflow: LLM calls on predefined code paths. Agent: the LLM dynamically decides its own steps and tool use.

flashcards.front: When to use prompt chaining?
flashcards.back: When a task decomposes into fixed, sequential subtasks. Add programmatic gates between steps.

flashcards.front: When to use routing?
flashcards.back: When inputs fall into distinct categories that need different prompts, tools or models (e.g. simple queries to a cheaper model).

flashcards.front: Parallelization: two variants?
flashcards.back: Sectioning (independent subtasks run concurrently) and voting (the same task run multiple times for confidence or diversity).

flashcards.front: Orchestrator-workers vs parallelization?
flashcards.back: The orchestrator decides the subtasks dynamically from the input. Parallelization uses predefined subtasks.

flashcards.front: When is evaluator-optimizer worthwhile?
flashcards.back: When clear evaluation criteria exist and iterative critique measurably improves output.

flashcards.front: Main benefit of subagents?
flashcards.back: Context isolation (each has its own fresh window), plus parallelism and specialization with restricted tools.

flashcards.front: Does a subagent see the orchestrator's conversation?
flashcards.back: No. Its delegation prompt must include all the context, scope, output format and effort guidance.

flashcards.front: What should workers return to an orchestrator?
flashcards.back: Condensed, structured findings with provenance, not raw dumps.

flashcards.front: When is a multi-agent system a poor fit?
flashcards.back: Tightly coupled tasks with shared evolving state (many edits to the same code), or simple tasks where token cost isn't justified.

flashcards.front: Where should a hard business limit (e.g. max refund) be enforced?
flashcards.back: In code: tool-side validation, hooks or permission checks. Not just in the prompt.

flashcards.front: What should an escalation handoff include?
flashcards.back: A structured summary: customer or context, the request, actions tried, current state, and the specific decision needed.

flashcards.front: Partial resolution?
flashcards.back: Complete the safe, in-policy parts and escalate only the part that needs human approval.

flashcards.front: What is the Claude Agent SDK?
flashcards.back: The Claude Code agent harness as a library (Python/TS): agent loop, tools, context management, subagents, hooks, permissions, sessions.

flashcards.front: How are custom tools typically added in the Agent SDK?
flashcards.back: As MCP servers, including in-process SDK MCP servers.

flashcards.front: When is bypassing permissions acceptable?
flashcards.back: Only in isolated sandboxes (containers or VMs with scoped credentials).

flashcards.front: Typical escalation triggers?
flashcards.back: Policy limit exceeded, explicit request for a human, sensitive category, low confidence after bounded attempts, repeated tool failure, loop guard tripped.

flashcards.front: What does stop_reason "pause_turn" mean, and how do you continue?
flashcards.back: A server-tool loop (run on Anthropic's side) hit its per-request iteration limit. Send the assistant content back as-is, plus the container id if present. Client tool_use never produces it.

flashcards.front: How does a refusal show up in the API?
flashcards.back: HTTP 200 with stop_reason "refusal". stop_details is set only for refusals. Read it and, where appropriate, retry on a fallback model; do not loop on the same request.

flashcards.front: What does stop_reason "model_context_window_exceeded" mean?
flashcards.back: Generation stopped because the context window filled. Treat it like max_tokens: the output is truncated, not finished.

flashcards.front: Common cause of an empty end_turn response after tool use?
flashcards.back: Adding text after the tool_result blocks. Fix the message shape instead of retrying unchanged; as a last resort send a new "Please continue" user message.

flashcards.front: Why code a default branch in the stop_reason switch?
flashcards.back: New stop reasons get added. Unknown values should be logged and handled as abnormal, not silently treated as success.

flashcards.front: Agent SDK result subtypes?
flashcards.back: success, error_max_turns, error_max_budget_usd, error_during_execution, error_max_structured_output_retries. Only success carries the result field.

flashcards.front: Agent SDK: allowed_tools vs disallowed_tools?
flashcards.back: allowed_tools auto-approves the listed tools but does not hide the others. disallowed_tools blocks tools regardless of other settings.

flashcards.front: Can an Agent SDK run spend more than max_budget_usd?
flashcards.back: Yes, by up to one response. Leave headroom and handle error_max_budget_usd.

flashcards.front: What does the dontAsk permission mode do?
flashcards.back: Auto-denies any tool call that would otherwise prompt for approval. Useful for unattended runs where no human can answer.

flashcards.front: Can Claude Code subagents spawn subagents?
flashcards.back: Yes. By default up to 3 layers below the main conversation (CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH; 1 disables nesting).

flashcards.front: Subagent vs fork: what context does each start with?
flashcards.back: A normal subagent starts fresh and returns only its summary. A fork inherits the parent conversation.

flashcards.front: What happens if a Claude Code subagent definition omits tools?
flashcards.back: It inherits all tools available to subagents, including MCP tools. Set tools or disallowedTools for least privilege.

flashcards.front: Static vs dynamic task decomposition?
flashcards.back: Static: subtasks known in advance and written in code (chaining, sectioning). Dynamic: an orchestrator or agent plans subtasks at runtime from the input and findings.

flashcards.front: Three failure classes and the response to each?
flashcards.back: Transient: bounded backoff retry. Correctable: return is_error with an instructive message so Claude fixes the call. Persistent/policy: stop, report, escalate.

flashcards.front: Is CLAUDE.md (even managed CLAUDE.md) an enforcement mechanism?
flashcards.back: No. It is context. Enforce with PreToolUse hooks, managed permissions.deny, sandboxing or tool-side code.

flashcards.front: Do Agent SDK hooks consume context tokens?
flashcards.back: No. Hooks run in your own process, which makes them a cheap, deterministic place for logging and policy.

flashcards.front: Which Agent SDK tools run concurrently?
flashcards.back: Read-only ones (Read, Glob, Grep, MCP tools marked read-only). Edit, Write and Bash run one at a time.

flashcards.front: User-level CLAUDE.md location?
flashcards.back: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md: personal preferences for all projects.

flashcards.front: Where do team conventions go?
flashcards.back: The project CLAUDE.md (repo root or .claude/CLAUDE.md), committed to git.

flashcards.front: How are subdirectory CLAUDE.md files used?
flashcards.back: Loaded when Claude works with files in that subtree, which suits monorepo packages.

flashcards.front: CLAUDE.md import syntax?
flashcards.back: @path/to/file (e.g. @docs/architecture.md, @~/.claude/prefs.md).

flashcards.front: What are .claude/rules/ files?
flashcards.back: Modular instruction files, optionally path-scoped via frontmatter globs so they apply only to matching files.

flashcards.front: Command to bootstrap CLAUDE.md?
flashcards.back: /init

flashcards.front: Settings precedence in Claude Code?
flashcards.back: Managed > command-line flags > project local > shared project > user. Array settings like permissions.allow merge across scopes.

flashcards.front: allow vs deny conflict?
flashcards.back: deny wins. Rules are checked deny, then ask, then allow; the first match wins regardless of specificity.

flashcards.front: Which settings file is personal and git-ignored?
flashcards.back: .claude/settings.local.json

flashcards.front: Hook to block a dangerous tool call?
flashcards.back: PreToolUse: exit code 2 (stderr fed back to Claude) or return permissionDecision "deny". Exit 1 does not block.

flashcards.front: Hook to auto-format after every edit?
flashcards.back: PostToolUse with a matcher such as Edit|Write.

flashcards.front: CLAUDE.md instruction vs hook?
flashcards.back: CLAUDE.md: guidance the model should follow. Hook: deterministic, runs every time.

flashcards.front: What is a Skill?
flashcards.back: A folder at .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md (or ~/.claude/skills/) plus optional scripts and resources. Only the description stays in context; the body loads when invoked.

flashcards.front: Custom slash commands vs skills today?
flashcards.back: Merged. .claude/commands/x.md and .claude/skills/x/SKILL.md both create /x; skills are preferred (bundled files, model invocation).

flashcards.front: Subagent definition location and key fields?
flashcards.back: .claude/agents/<name>.md: only name and description are required; tools, model, permissionMode, maxTurns etc. are optional; body is the system prompt.

flashcards.front: What does plan mode do?
flashcards.back: Read-only exploration and a proposed plan; no edits until you approve. Enter via Shift+Tab, /plan or --permission-mode plan.

flashcards.front: Why does a CI job running `claude "..."` hang?
flashcards.back: Without -p it starts an interactive session waiting for input. Use claude -p.

flashcards.front: Machine-readable headless output flag?
flashcards.back: --output-format json (or stream-json).

flashcards.front: How to pre-approve tools in headless runs?
flashcards.back: --allowedTools (e.g. "Read,Bash(npm run test *)"), --disallowedTools, or permission rules in committed settings.

flashcards.front: How to set up the Claude GitHub Action quickly?
flashcards.back: Run /install-github-app in Claude Code; it sets up the app, the anthropics/claude-code-action@v1 workflow and the secret.

flashcards.front: /clear vs /compact?
flashcards.back: /clear wipes the conversation context (new task). /compact summarizes history to free context while keeping key info.

flashcards.front: Recommended loop for complex coding tasks?
flashcards.back: Explore, then plan, then code, then verify (tests or linters), often starting in plan mode.

flashcards.front: How to keep secrets out of Claude Code's reach?
flashcards.back: deny rules (e.g. Read(./.env)), plus hooks and sandboxing. Not just instructions.

flashcards.front: Do multiple CLAUDE.md files override each other?
flashcards.back: No. Files from the filesystem root down to the cwd are concatenated; CLAUDE.local.md is appended after CLAUDE.md at each level.

flashcards.front: Where do personal, repo-specific notes go?
flashcards.back: ./CLAUDE.local.md, kept out of git.

flashcards.front: When does Claude Code read AGENTS.md?
flashcards.back: When no CLAUDE.md or CLAUDE.local.md exists in the cwd or above (recent versions).

flashcards.front: Max @import depth in CLAUDE.md?
flashcards.back: 4 hops. Imports organize memory but do not reduce context cost.

flashcards.front: Is the managed CLAUDE.md an enforcement mechanism?
flashcards.back: No, it is guidance. Enforce with managed settings (permissions.deny, sandbox) or hooks.

flashcards.front: How do you path-scope a .claude/rules file?
flashcards.back: YAML frontmatter `paths:` with globs (brace expansion allowed). It loads only when Claude reads or edits a matching file.

flashcards.front: Which permission modes cannot be set from project or local settings?
flashcards.back: auto and bypassPermissions (as defaultMode).

flashcards.front: How do admins stop anyone using bypassPermissions?
flashcards.back: permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode: "disable" in managed settings.

flashcards.front: What permission mode does claude -p start in?
flashcards.back: Manual (default): calls needing approval are denied unless a rule, flag or mode approves them.

flashcards.front: What does --bare do?
flashcards.back: Skips hooks, skills, plugins, MCP, auto memory and CLAUDE.md for a reproducible headless run; recommended for CI.

flashcards.front: Where does --json-schema output land?
flashcards.back: In structured_output of the --output-format json result; absent if no valid output, so check for it.

flashcards.front: How do you pass CLI flags to claude-code-action@v1?
flashcards.back: The claude_args input, e.g. "--max-turns 5 --allowedTools Read,Grep".

flashcards.front: Which files make Claude Code config shareable with a team?
flashcards.back: .claude/settings.json, .mcp.json, .claude/skills/, .claude/agents/, CLAUDE.md and .claude/rules/, all committed.

flashcards.front: Four ways to enter plan mode?
flashcards.back: Shift+Tab, /plan <prompt>, --permission-mode plan, "defaultMode": "plan".

flashcards.front: Why use XML tags in prompts?
flashcards.back: To separate instructions from data and structure outputs. Easier for Claude to follow and for code to parse.

flashcards.front: How many few-shot examples, and what kind?
flashcards.back: Typically 3–5, diverse and representative, including edge cases, wrapped in <example> tags.

flashcards.front: Role of the system prompt?
flashcards.back: Role, standing context, constraints and tone. The task goes in the user turn.

flashcards.front: Why explain the reason behind an instruction?
flashcards.back: Claude generalizes better from motivation than from bare rules.

flashcards.front: Problem with ever-growing IF-THEN prompts?
flashcards.back: Brittle, conflicting rules and instruction dilution. Prefer principles plus examples, or split and route.

flashcards.front: When to use extended thinking, and how on current models?
flashcards.back: Complex reasoning, math, multi-step analysis. On current models use adaptive thinking with output_config.effort. Prompted step-by-step CoT is a fallback for models without thinking.

flashcards.front: Most reliable ways to get schema-conformant JSON?
flashcards.back: Structured outputs (output_config.format with a JSON schema) or a tool with strict: true, plus validation in code. Forced tool_choice only on models that support it.

flashcards.front: Prefill caveat?
flashcards.back: Prefill is unsupported on Claude 4.6+ models and returns a 400. Use structured outputs or instructions instead.

flashcards.front: How to reduce fabricated fields in extraction?
flashcards.back: Nullable or optional fields plus an explicit "use null if absent; don't guess".

flashcards.front: Validation failed. What next?
flashcards.back: Retry with the specific validation errors as feedback, bounded. Then route to human review.

flashcards.front: Does valid JSON mean correct data?
flashcards.back: No. Add business-rule checks, provenance (quotes, pages) and review for low confidence.

flashcards.front: Positive vs negative instructions?
flashcards.back: Say what to do ("write in prose paragraphs"), not only what not to do.

flashcards.front: Why version prompts?
flashcards.back: To track changes and compare versions against evals before shipping, like code.

flashcards.front: Enum design tip for classification?
flashcards.back: Include an "other" or "unknown" option plus a detail field so the model isn't forced into a wrong class.

flashcards.front: When is tag-separated CoT (<thinking> then <answer>) still appropriate?
flashcards.back: As a fallback on models without built-in thinking, with code parsing <answer>. On the newest models, asking for visible reasoning can trigger a reasoning_extraction refusal.

flashcards.front: Prompt chaining advantage for complex tasks?
flashcards.back: Each step is focused, inspectable and retryable. Intermediate outputs can be validated.

flashcards.front: Few-shot pitfall?
flashcards.back: Examples that share accidental patterns (same length or same label) that the model copies.

flashcards.front: Where do field-level instructions go in a tool schema?
flashcards.back: In each property's description, which acts as an instruction.

flashcards.front: Manual extended thinking on Claude 4.7+?
flashcards.back: Removed: thinking {type: "enabled"} returns a 400. Use thinking {type: "adaptive"} with output_config.effort.

flashcards.front: A simple task is slow on Opus 5.5, where thinking can't be disabled. What lever?
flashcards.back: Lower the effort level (output_config.effort).

flashcards.front: Why not ask the newest models for reasoning in <thinking> tags or a "reasoning" schema field?
flashcards.back: It may trigger a reasoning_extraction refusal. Rely on built-in thinking and ask for a short "explanation" instead.

flashcards.front: How do you request JSON outputs in the current API?
flashcards.back: output_config: {format: {type: "json_schema", schema: {...}}}. The older output_format parameter is deprecated.

flashcards.front: What does strict: true on a tool definition do?
flashcards.back: Constrained decoding makes the tool input conform to its input_schema.

flashcards.front: Schema rules for structured outputs?
flashcards.back: additionalProperties: false on every object. No numeric or string-length constraints and no recursive schemas, so check ranges in code.

flashcards.front: Can a structured-outputs response still fail to conform?
flashcards.back: Yes, on a refusal or max_tokens stop. Check stop_reason before trusting the JSON.

flashcards.front: Forced tool_choice ("tool" or "any") on the newest flagship models?
flashcards.back: Not supported (400). Use auto with strict: true tools, or structured outputs.

flashcards.front: Where do long documents and the query go?
flashcards.back: Documents at the top, the query at the end (reported up to 30% better). Ask for relevant quotes first.

flashcards.front: Effect of "CRITICAL: You MUST..." on newer models?
flashcards.back: It tends to overtrigger. Use calm, direct wording with the reason.

flashcards.front: What is a prompt regression eval?
flashcards.back: A fixed, representative case set with pass criteria, rerun on every prompt or model change and compared with the baseline before shipping.

flashcards.front: A tool call has invalid input. What do you return?
flashcards.back: A tool_result with is_error: true and the specific error text. Claude usually corrects and retries.

flashcards.front: Side effects of changing output_config.format?
flashcards.back: It invalidates the prompt cache, and a new schema adds grammar-compile latency on first use.

flashcards.front: Most important part of a tool definition?
flashcards.back: The description: what it does, when (and when not) to use it, parameter meanings and formats, return value, limits.

flashcards.front: tool_choice options?
flashcards.back: auto (model decides; default with tools), any (must use some tool), tool (must use the named tool), none (default with no tools). any/tool return 400 on the newest models.

flashcards.front: How to guarantee schema-shaped JSON output on current models?
flashcards.back: Use structured outputs (output_config.format) or a strict: true tool with tool_choice auto. Forcing a tool with tool_choice {type: "tool"} works only on models that still support forced tool use.

flashcards.front: How to report a tool failure to Claude?
flashcards.back: A tool_result with is_error: true and an actionable message (what failed, whether to retry, what to do instead).

flashcards.front: Why not return an empty string on tool failure?
flashcards.back: The model may read it as "no results" and proceed wrongly or fabricate.

flashcards.front: Transient vs permanent tool errors?
flashcards.back: Transient (timeouts, 429/5xx): retry with backoff in code. Permanent (validation, not found, forbidden): return the error immediately with guidance.

flashcards.front: Payment call timed out. Retry?
flashcards.back: Not blindly. Check status first, or retry with the same idempotency key.

flashcards.front: Why limit the number of tools?
flashcards.back: Overlapping or excessive tools hurt selection accuracy and consume context on every request.

flashcards.front: Design tools around ___ rather than ___.
flashcards.back: The agent's tasks rather than mirroring every API endpoint.

flashcards.front: Why nullable fields in tool schemas?
flashcards.back: So the model can express "unknown" instead of inventing values.

flashcards.front: Parallel tool calls: how to return results?
flashcards.back: One tool_result per tool_use id, all together in the next user message, with the tool_result blocks before any text.

flashcards.front: MCP tools / resources / prompts: who controls each?
flashcards.back: Tools: model-controlled. Resources: application-controlled. Prompts: user-controlled.

flashcards.front: MCP transports?
flashcards.back: stdio (local subprocess) and Streamable HTTP (remote, OAuth recommended). Standalone SSE is deprecated.

flashcards.front: Claude Code MCP scopes?
flashcards.back: Local (you, this project; default; ~/.claude.json), project (.mcp.json committed for the team), user (you, all projects; ~/.claude.json).

flashcards.front: How to share an MCP server config with a team without leaking secrets?
flashcards.back: Project scope .mcp.json with environment-variable expansion for credentials.

flashcards.front: Main MCP security risk?
flashcards.back: Untrusted servers or content: code execution and prompt injection via tool results. Use trusted servers, least privilege and approval gates.

flashcards.front: How are MCP tools named in Claude Code permissions?
flashcards.back: mcp__<server>__<tool>, which can appear in allow or deny rules.

flashcards.front: MCP sampling, roots and logging: current status?
flashcards.back: Deprecated as of protocol revision 2026-07-28. Sampling let a server request a completion through the client; roots were advisory hints, never a security boundary. Elicitation remains.

flashcards.front: Idempotency key purpose?
flashcards.back: Makes retries of side-effecting operations safe: the server deduplicates repeated requests.

flashcards.front: What should a tool return?
flashcards.back: Compact, relevant, human-readable fields. Paginate or truncate large results with a note.

flashcards.front: MCP host vs client vs server?
flashcards.back: Host: the AI application. Client: created by the host, one per server, holding a 1:1 connection. Server: exposes tools, resources and prompts.

flashcards.front: MCP layers?
flashcards.back: Data layer: JSON-RPC 2.0 messages (tools/list, tools/call, resources/read, prompts/get). Transport layer: stdio or Streamable HTTP.

flashcards.front: MCP elicitation modes?
flashcards.back: Form mode (structured fields) and URL mode (send the user to a page). URL mode is for sensitive data.

flashcards.front: Are MCP roots a security boundary?
flashcards.back: No. They were advisory hints, and are deprecated in 2026-07-28. Enforce access with permissions, sandboxing or the server.

flashcards.front: What made MCP 2026-07-28 "stateless"?
flashcards.back: Each request carries version and capabilities in _meta; servers implement server/discover; change notifications are opt-in via subscriptions/listen.

flashcards.front: tool_choice any/tool on Opus 5.5 or Sonnet 5.5?
flashcards.back: Returns 400: forced tool use is not supported. Use auto plus strict: true, or structured outputs.

flashcards.front: What does forcing a tool (any/tool) skip?
flashcards.back: Any text or thinking before the tool_use block, because the API prefills the turn. Manual extended thinking is incompatible with forcing.

flashcards.front: disable_parallel_tool_use: true does what?
flashcards.back: Limits Claude to at most one tool call per turn.

flashcards.front: Where do tool_result blocks go?
flashcards.back: In the user message right after the tool call, first in its content; any text comes after. Text before them returns 400.

flashcards.front: Claude Code MCP scope precedence?
flashcards.back: local > project > user > plugin > claude.ai connectors. The winning entry is used whole; fields do not merge.

flashcards.front: Add a remote MCP server in Claude Code?
flashcards.back: claude mcp add --transport http <name> <url>. (sse is deprecated.)

flashcards.front: How are MCP tool names formed in Claude Code?
flashcards.back: mcp__<server>__<tool>, usable in allow and deny permission rules.

flashcards.front: Why namespace tool names (github_list_prs)?
flashcards.back: It keeps tools distinct when many servers or services coexist, improving selection.

flashcards.front: response_format parameter on a tool?
flashcards.back: An enum such as concise | detailed so the agent requests only the detail it needs; concise saves many tokens.

flashcards.front: input_examples on a tool definition?
flashcards.back: Optional example inputs that show correct usage; they must validate against input_schema or the request fails, and they cost tokens.

flashcards.front: Where should fetched web content go in the request?
flashcards.back: Inside tool_result blocks, treated as untrusted data. Never in the system prompt.

flashcards.front: MCP output limits in Claude Code?
flashcards.back: Warning above about 10,000 tokens; a default maximum (25,000) adjustable with MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS.

flashcards.front: MCP OAuth in claude -p or the Agent SDK?
flashcards.back: Those runs cannot complete an OAuth flow (OAuth runs through /mcp in interactive sessions). Supply credentials another way, such as a header token from an environment variable.

flashcards.front: Long documents: where in the prompt?
flashcards.back: At the top, with the question or instructions at the end.

flashcards.front: How to ground answers in long documents?
flashcards.back: Ask Claude to extract relevant quotes first, then answer from them, or use citations.

flashcards.front: Why can a single key detail be missed in a very long context?
flashcards.back: Recall degrades as the context fills (context rot), so a detail buried in lots of irrelevant text is easy to miss. Retrieve and order deliberately.

flashcards.front: Prompt caching marker?
flashcards.back: cache_control: {"type": "ephemeral"} on the last block of the stable prefix.

flashcards.front: Cache prefix order?
flashcards.back: tools, then system, then messages. Stable content first, variable content after the breakpoint.

flashcards.front: Why might a cache never hit?
flashcards.back: Something variable (timestamp, user name) sits before the breakpoint, so the prefix changes every call.

flashcards.front: Cache pricing intuition?
flashcards.back: Writes cost more than normal input (more again for the 1-hour TTL). Reads cost a small fraction of normal input. Hits also cut latency.

flashcards.front: What is compaction?
flashcards.back: Summarizing older context to free space while preserving decisions, state and open tasks.

flashcards.front: How do long-running agents survive context limits?
flashcards.back: External memory (plan or progress files, memory tool), compaction, subagents, resumable sessions.

flashcards.front: Why use an independent reviewer instance?
flashcards.back: A fresh context is not anchored on the author's reasoning and checks against the original requirements (as in the evaluator-optimizer pattern). Pair it with deterministic checks.

flashcards.front: Retry policy for 429 / 529?
flashcards.back: Exponential backoff with jitter, honour retry-after, cap attempts. SDKs retry automatically.

flashcards.front: When to use the Message Batches API?
flashcards.back: Large, non-urgent workloads: asynchronous processing at about half the cost. Most finish within an hour; batches expire after 24 hours.

flashcards.front: Critical constraint drifting in a long session?
flashcards.back: Early chat rules can be diluted or compacted away. Keep them in the system prompt or CLAUDE.md, or enforce them in code.

flashcards.front: Provenance requirement in research agents?
flashcards.back: Every claim carries a source (URL, doc id, quote) so it can be verified and conflicts resolved.

flashcards.front: Types of eval grading?
flashcards.back: Code-graded (exact match, schema, tests), LLM-as-judge with a rubric, human grading.

flashcards.front: How do you reduce hallucination cheaply?
flashcards.back: Allow "I don't know", ground in provided documents, require quotes or citations.

flashcards.front: Why trim tool outputs?
flashcards.back: Large raw outputs consume context, raise cost and bury relevant facts.

flashcards.front: Usage fields that show caching works?
flashcards.back: cache_creation_input_tokens (written) and cache_read_input_tokens (hit).

flashcards.front: Model routing for cost and latency?
flashcards.back: Send simple steps to smaller, faster models and hard reasoning to larger models.

flashcards.front: What should an eval set look like?
flashcards.back: Representative real-world cases including edge cases, with clear success criteria. Run it on every change.

flashcards.front: How many cache breakpoints per request?
flashcards.back: Up to 4. Automatic (top-level) caching uses one of those slots.

flashcards.front: Prompt cache lifetime?
flashcards.back: 5 minutes by default, refreshed on each hit. A 1-hour TTL is available for longer gaps between requests.

flashcards.front: Prompt shorter than the minimum cacheable length?
flashcards.back: It is simply not cached. No error is returned; cache_creation_input_tokens stays 0.

flashcards.front: Which change invalidates the entire prompt cache?
flashcards.back: Changing tool definitions, because tools are the first part of the prefix.

flashcards.front: Changing tool_choice, images or thinking parameters invalidates what?
flashcards.back: The cached messages only; cached tools and system stay valid.

flashcards.front: "Context rot"?
flashcards.back: Recall degrades as the window fills. Treat context as a finite attention budget: the smallest set of high-signal tokens.

flashcards.front: Just-in-time retrieval?
flashcards.back: Keep lightweight references (paths, queries, ids) in context and load the data with tools when needed.

flashcards.front: Lightest-touch form of compaction?
flashcards.back: Clearing old tool results that have already been used.

flashcards.front: What should a sub-agent return to its parent?
flashcards.back: A condensed summary (often about 1,000 to 2,000 tokens) with sources, not its full history.

flashcards.front: Structured note-taking?
flashcards.back: The agent writes progress to a file such as NOTES.md and reads it back after a reset or compaction.
429 rate_limit_error: your limits. 529 overloaded_error: load across all users. Both are transient: back off with jitter.

flashcards.front: A 429 with no retry-after that never clears?
flashcards.back: Likely a spend cap. Stop retrying, alert, and surface the error.

flashcards.front: Do the Claude SDKs retry automatically?
flashcards.back: Yes: connection errors, 429 and 5xx, twice by default with backoff, honouring retry-after. Configure max_retries.

flashcards.front: How do you match Message Batches results to requests?
flashcards.back: By custom_id. Results can arrive in any order.

flashcards.front: Which batch results are billed?
flashcards.back: Only succeeded requests. Resubmit errored or expired ones.

flashcards.front: Very long API requests?
flashcards.back: Use streaming or the Batches API rather than one long blocking request.

flashcards.front: Why can a self-review in the same session miss bugs?
flashcards.back: The context already holds the author's reasoning, so it is anchored on it (a design judgment). Use a fresh instance with the requirements and a rubric.

flashcards.front: What survives /compact in Claude Code?
flashcards.back: The project-root CLAUDE.md is re-read; rules stated only in early chat turns may be summarized away.

questions.scenario: Customer support agent with tools and escalation
questions.stem: A support agent loops over the Messages API. The team detects completion by checking whether the assistant's text contains "RESOLVED". In production, some sessions end before refunds are processed and others loop forever. What is the best fix?
options: Add a stronger system prompt instruction to always end with the word RESOLVED
Ask the model to output a JSON status field on every turn and parse it
Reduce max_turns to 3 so loops can't run forever
Drive the loop from stop_reason: execute tools on "tool_use" and finish on "end_turn", handling other stop reasons explicitly
questions.explanation: stop_reason is the structured, reliable control signal for the agent loop. Text markers are fragile: the model can emit them early or never. Iteration caps only bound the damage.
rationales: Still relies on parsing free text, which stays unreliable no matter how strongly it's worded.
Self-reported status is still model text. stop_reason already exists for this.
A cap is a safety net. It would cut legitimate multi-step work short and doesn't detect completion.
Correct. It uses the API's structured signal for tool requests and completion.

questions.stem: An agent occasionally returns half-finished JSON reports that fail parsing downstream. Logs show these responses have stop_reason "max_tokens". What should the architect do?
options: Switch to a larger model, which never truncates
Wrap the JSON parser in try/except and drop the malformed reports
Add "keep your answer short" to the system prompt
Treat max_tokens as truncation: raise max_tokens or continue generation, and never parse output that stopped this way as final
questions.explanation: max_tokens means the output hit the configured limit and is incomplete. The fix is detecting the condition and either raising the limit or continuing, not hiding failures or hoping the model is brief.
rationales: Any model truncates when it reaches max_tokens. The limit is yours.
Silently drops data and hides the root cause.
Might reduce frequency, but doesn't handle the condition and may hurt report quality.
Correct. It detects and handles truncation explicitly.

sources.title: Handling stop reasons — Claude API docs

questions.stem: A research agent sometimes runs 200+ tool calls on hard questions, burning budget. The team proposes max_turns=15 as the way the agent "knows it's finished". What is the best architectural response?
options: Accept it, since max_turns is the standard completion mechanism in the Agent SDK
Remove all limits so the agent can always finish
Keep completion on end_turn, add max_turns/budget limits as a safety net, and treat hitting them as an abnormal outcome that returns partial results and is logged
Ask the agent to count its own tool calls and stop at 15
questions.explanation: Hard caps protect against runaways but are not the completion signal. When a cap trips, the system should handle that as an exception path, returning partial results with a flag and logging it, while normal completion stays on end_turn.
rationales: Wrong. max_turns is a guard, not the completion signal.
Correct. A safety net plus explicit handling of the abnormal outcome.
Model self-counting is unreliable. Enforce limits in code.

questions.scenario: Customer support agent with tools and escalation
questions.stem: Claude returns two tool_use blocks (get_order and get_customer) in one response. How should the application respond?
options: Execute only the first tool and send its result. Claude will request the second next turn
Execute both and send two separate user messages, one per result
Execute both and return the results as plain text in an assistant message
Execute both and send a single user message containing a tool_result block for each tool_use id
questions.explanation: With parallel tool use, every tool_use id needs a corresponding tool_result, and they go together in the next user message.
rationales: Missing tool results for an emitted tool_use id cause an API error.
Results belong together in one user message.
Tool results go in the user role as tool_result blocks.

questions.stem: Every incoming invoice must be (1) OCR-cleaned, (2) field-extracted, (3) validated against the PO system and (4) summarized. The steps never change. Which architecture fits best?
options: An autonomous agent with all four capabilities as tools, deciding its own order
Prompt chaining: a fixed sequence of focused calls with programmatic validation gates between steps
An orchestrator-workers system that dynamically plans subtasks per invoice
A single prompt asking Claude to do all four steps at once
questions.explanation: Fixed, known steps are the textbook case for prompt chaining. It is predictable, testable and cheaper, and gates catch errors between steps. An agent's flexibility isn't needed.
rationales: Adds unpredictability and cost for no benefit when the order is fixed.
Dynamic planning is for subtasks that can't be known in advance.
A monolithic prompt can't be validated between steps and is harder to debug.

questions.scenario: Customer support agent with tools and escalation
questions.stem: A support system receives billing disputes, technical bugs and general product questions. Each needs a different prompt and tool set, and 60% are simple FAQs. Which pattern best fits?
options: Routing: classify each request, then dispatch it to a specialized prompt/tool set, sending simple FAQs to a smaller, faster model
Voting: run every request through three models and take the majority answer
Evaluator-optimizer: generate an answer and refine it until a judge approves
A single generalist agent with every tool available
questions.explanation: Distinct categories that need different handling are what routing is for. It also enables cost optimization by sending easy traffic to cheaper models.
rationales: Triples cost and doesn't specialize the handling.
Useful for quality refinement, but not for dispatching distinct categories.
Tool bloat and a diluted prompt reduce accuracy, and every request pays for the largest model.

questions.stem: What distinguishes orchestrator-workers from the sectioning form of parallelization?
options: Orchestrator-workers always runs workers sequentially
Sectioning requires a different model per subtask
In orchestrator-workers, the central LLM decides the subtasks dynamically based on the input. In sectioning, the subtasks are predefined
Sectioning can only be used for voting on the same task
questions.explanation: Both can run work in parallel. The key difference is who defines the subtasks: predefined in code for sectioning, decided at runtime by the orchestrator for orchestrator-workers.
rationales: Voting is the other form of parallelization. Sectioning splits distinct subtasks.

questions.stem: A code-translation pipeline produces output that often compiles but fails style and test checks. Clear, automatable acceptance criteria exist. Which pattern most directly improves quality?
options: Routing between two translation prompts
Increase temperature to explore more solutions
A single larger prompt with all the style rules inline
Evaluator-optimizer: generate, evaluate against the criteria (tests, style), feed back the specific failures, and iterate within a bound
questions.explanation: Evaluator-optimizer works when clear criteria exist and iterative feedback measurably improves the output. Here the tests and linters provide objective feedback.
rationales: More randomness doesn't fix systematic failures.
Doesn't verify the output. Instruction dilution may get worse.

questions.stem: An orchestrator delegates "research competitor pricing" to three subagents. They return overlapping, shallow results, and one researches the wrong company. What is the most likely root cause and fix?
options: The subagents need a larger model. Upgrade all three
Run the subagents sequentially so each can read the previous one's output
Subagents should share one context window so they can coordinate
The delegation prompts were vague. Give each subagent a complete brief with objective, scope boundaries, expected output format and effort guidance, since subagents don't see the parent's context
questions.explanation: Subagents start with fresh context and know only what the delegation prompt tells them. Overlap and drift come from underspecified briefs.
rationales: Model size doesn't fix missing context.
Slower, and still doesn't fix the vague tasks.
That defeats context isolation, which is the main benefit of subagents.

questions.stem: Subagents return full HTML of every page they read to the orchestrator, which then runs out of context. What should change?
options: Compress the HTML with gzip before returning it
Switch the orchestrator to a model with a larger context window and keep the raw HTML
Stop using subagents and have the orchestrator read all pages itself
Workers should return condensed, structured findings with source citations instead of raw content
questions.explanation: The point of subagents is to absorb heavy context and return distilled results. Citations keep provenance without the bulk.
rationales: The model consumes tokens, not compressed bytes. This doesn't help.
Postpones the problem, and irrelevant context still degrades quality.
Makes the orchestrator's context problem worse.

questions.stem: A team wants to parallelize a refactor by giving five subagents different steps of a change that touches the same tightly coupled modules. What is the best guidance?
options: Proceed, since more agents always finish faster
Use voting: have all five do the full refactor and pick the best
Multi-agent parallelism fits poorly for tightly coupled edits to shared state. Prefer a single agent (optionally with subagents for read-only investigation) working sequentially with tests
Give each subagent write access to separate copies of the repo and merge at the end without review
questions.explanation: Multi-agent systems shine for breadth-first, independent work. Tightly coupled changes need shared, evolving context, and parallel writers create conflicts.
rationales: Coordination costs and conflicts can make it slower and worse.
Five times the cost, and it doesn't address coupling.
Unreviewed merges of conflicting changes are risky.

questions.scenario: Customer support agent with tools and escalation
questions.stem: Company policy: agents may never issue refunds above $500 without manager approval. In testing, the agent sometimes ignores the system prompt rule. What is the best design?
options: Repeat the rule three times in the system prompt in capital letters
Add a few-shot example of refusing a $600 refund
Lower the temperature to 0
Enforce the limit in the refund tool's handler: reject amounts over $500 with a structured "approval required" result that routes to escalation
questions.explanation: Must-never business rules with financial impact belong in deterministic code. Prompts guide behaviour, but code guarantees it.

questions.scenario: Customer support agent with tools and escalation
questions.stem: A customer asks for an order status update AND a $900 refund. Refunds over $500 need approval. What should the agent do?
options: Escalate the entire conversation to a human immediately
Provide the order status, explain the refund needs approval, and create an escalation with a structured summary for the refund part only
Issue a $500 refund now and tell the customer the rest is unavailable
Refuse both requests until a manager joins
questions.explanation: Partial resolution: do the safe, in-policy work and escalate only the part that needs a human, with a structured handoff.
rationales: Wastes human time on what the agent can handle.
Acts outside policy and the customer's request.
Poor experience. The status lookup is safe.

questions.scenario: Customer support agent with tools and escalation
questions.stem: When the support agent escalates to a human, what should the handoff include?
options: Only a link to the raw transcript
Just the customer's last message
A structured summary: customer identity, the request, actions already taken, current state, and the specific decision needed
The agent's full system prompt
questions.explanation: A structured summary lets the human act quickly without rereading the conversation.
rationales: Forces the human to reconstruct the context.

questions.scenario: Customer support agent with tools and escalation
questions.stem: Which are good, testable escalation triggers for a support agent? (Select two.)
options: The customer explicitly asks to speak to a human
The model "feels" the conversation is going badly
A requested action exceeds a policy limit enforced by the tool
The conversation exceeds 3 messages
questions.explanation: Good triggers are explicit and verifiable: explicit requests for a human and policy limits. A vague feeling isn't testable, and an arbitrary message count escalates normal conversations.
rationales: Correct. Deterministic and enforced in code.
An arbitrary threshold that escalates normal conversations.

questions.scenario: Developer productivity tooling for a team
questions.stem: A team builds an internal agent with the Claude Agent SDK that can run shell commands. Security requires that `rm -rf` and writes outside the workspace are always blocked and logged. What is the best mechanism?
options: A system prompt instruction listing forbidden commands
A PostToolUse hook that reverts damage after the command runs
Ask the agent to confirm with itself before each command
A PreToolUse hook / permission callback that inspects each Bash call, denies matching commands deterministically and logs them
questions.explanation: PreToolUse hooks and permission callbacks run before execution and decide deterministically. Prompts are probabilistic, and post-hoc reversion is too late for destructive actions.
rationales: Runs after the damage is done.

questions.stem: When is it appropriate to run an agent with permission checks bypassed?
options: On developer laptops, to reduce permission prompts
Whenever the agent uses a trusted model
In production against live customer databases, for speed
Only inside an isolated sandbox (e.g. a container with no secrets and limited network) where damage is contained
questions.explanation: Bypassing permissions removes all approval checks. It's acceptable only when the environment itself contains the blast radius.
rationales: Laptops hold credentials and personal data.
Model trust doesn't remove the risk of mistakes or prompt injection.

sources.title: Agent SDK overview — Claude Code docs

questions.scenario: Developer productivity tooling for a team
questions.stem: What does the Claude Agent SDK primarily provide?
options: The same agent harness that powers Claude Code (agent loop, built-in tools, context management, hooks, permissions, subagents, sessions) as a library
A hosted UI for chatting with Claude
A fine-tuning service for custom Claude models
A vector database for retrieval
questions.explanation: The Agent SDK exposes the Claude Code harness programmatically for building custom agents.

sources.title: Agent SDK overview — Claude Code docs

questions.stem: A long-running research agent must survive context limits and process restarts over a multi-hour task. Which design choices help most? (Select two.)
options: Persist the plan, progress and findings to an external memory or plan file the agent reads and updates
Keep everything in the conversation so nothing is lost
Store session/message history and design steps to be resumable and idempotent
Lower max_tokens so each turn uses less context
questions.explanation: External memory and resumable, idempotent steps let work continue across compaction, new context windows and restarts.
rationales: The context window is finite, and restarts lose in-memory state.
Output size isn't the main issue, and truncation adds risk.

questions.stem: A team wants to extract fields from a single short form. They've designed a three-agent system (planner, extractor, verifier). What should the architect recommend first?
options: Add a fourth agent to coordinate the other three
Use voting with five extractor agents
Start with a single well-prompted call (schema plus examples plus validation in code), and add complexity only if evals show it's needed
Use an autonomous agent with web access
questions.explanation: The guidance is to use the simplest solution that works. Multi-agent systems add cost, latency and failure points, which you should justify with measured gains.

questions.scenario: Customer support agent with tools and escalation
questions.stem: A customer's tool call to look up an account fails three times with a timeout. What should the agent's design do next?
options: Keep retrying indefinitely until it works
Make up a plausible account status so the conversation can continue
Tell the customer their account doesn't exist
Stop retrying after the bounded attempts, tell the customer about the issue honestly, and escalate or offer a follow-up with context attached
questions.explanation: Repeated tool failure is a classic escalation trigger. Be honest, bounded and stateful.

sources.title: Handle tool calls — Claude API docs

questions.stem: An orchestrator gives every subagent the full tool set: web search, code execution, email sending and database write. What is the main architectural concern?
options: It prevents parallel execution
Subagents can't use more than three tools
Too many tools make responses shorter
It violates least privilege. Each worker should get only the tools its role needs, which reduces risk (including from prompt injection) and improves tool selection
questions.explanation: Least privilege limits blast radius and improves selection accuracy. A research worker reading untrusted web pages should not be able to send email.

questions.stem: A simple factual question ("What year was company X founded?") triggers the research orchestrator to spawn eight subagents. What should be improved?
options: Nothing. More agents means more accuracy
Remove subagents entirely from the system
Use only one model for all agents
Teach the orchestrator to scale effort to complexity: simple lookups use one agent or a few tool calls, broad surveys use many workers
questions.explanation: Effort-scaling rules in the orchestrator prompt prevent over-investment on simple queries while keeping parallelism for complex ones.
rationales: Loses the benefit for complex queries.

questions.scenario: Customer support agent with tools and escalation
questions.stem: Which actions should require human approval in an agentic customer system? (Select two.)
options: Issuing a large refund to a payment card
Reading the public FAQ
Permanently deleting a customer account
Looking up the order's shipping status
questions.explanation: Irreversible or high-impact actions (money movement, permanent deletion) warrant approval gates. Read-only lookups don't.

questions.scenario: Customer support agent with tools and escalation
questions.stem: A team stores conversation history only on the Anthropic side and expects follow-up Messages API calls to remember the user. Users complain the agent "forgets" everything. Why?
options: The model's memory resets every hour
The Messages API is stateless. The application must send the relevant conversation history (and system and tools) on every request
History is only kept when temperature is 0
The team must enable server-side memory in the model parameters
questions.explanation: The client owns state. Each request must include the history the model should consider.
rationales: Conversation state isn't kept automatically between Messages API calls.

sources.title: Handling stop reasons — Claude API docs

questions.scenario: Developer productivity tooling for a team
questions.stem: An Agent SDK automation ends with one of: success, max turns reached, budget exceeded, or permission denied. How should the system treat these?
options: All the same: return whatever text the agent last produced
Retry every non-success outcome with the same inputs automatically
Handle each terminal outcome explicitly: report success, flag partial results on limits, surface permission denials for review, and log all of them
Ignore permission denials. The agent will work around them
questions.explanation: Production agents need explicit handling per outcome for correctness and observability. In the Agent SDK the result subtype (success, error_max_turns, error_max_budget_usd, error_during_execution) tells you which path you are on. Limits deserve a flagged partial result, and permission denials are signals for review, not noise.
rationales: Blind retries waste money and repeat failures.

sources.title: Agent SDK overview — Claude Code docs

questions.stem: Five independent security checks (injection, auth, secrets, dependencies, logging) must each run over a PR, and latency matters. Which pattern fits best?
options: Prompt chaining, one check after another
Routing to the single most relevant check
An autonomous agent that decides which checks to run
Parallelization (sectioning): run the five focused checks concurrently, then aggregate
questions.explanation: Independent, predefined subtasks plus latency sensitivity point to sectioning-style parallelization. Focused prompts per check also improve attention.
rationales: Serializes independent work, so it's slower.
Unnecessary unpredictability for a fixed set of checks.

questions.stem: A research agent uses a server-side web search tool. Some responses come back with stop_reason "pause_turn" and no final answer, and the loop returns them to users as finished. What should the loop do on "pause_turn"?
options: Treat it as a refusal and retry the request on a fallback model
Execute the server tool locally and send a tool_result block for it
Raise max_tokens, because pause_turn means the output was truncated
Append the assistant content as-is (including the container id if present) and call the API again so the server-tool loop can continue
questions.explanation: pause_turn means a server-tool loop reached its per-request iteration limit. The documented way to continue is to send the assistant content back unchanged, plus any container id. It is not truncation, a refusal, or a client tool request.
rationales: Refusals have their own stop_reason and stop_details; this is not one.
Server tools run on Anthropic's side; there is no client tool_use to answer.
That handles max_tokens, a different condition.
Correct. Resending lets the paused server-side work resume.

sources.title: Handling stop reasons — Claude API docs

questions.stem: An extraction pipeline occasionally gets HTTP 200 responses with stop_reason "refusal" on certain documents. The current code resends the identical request up to 10 times. What is the better design?
options: Rely on the SDK's automatic retries, since refusals are retried like 5xx errors
Parse whatever partial content came back and mark the record as extracted
Handle refusal as its own outcome: read stop_details, retry once on a fallback model where appropriate, and otherwise route the document for review
Increase max_tokens so the model has room to complete the extraction
questions.explanation: A refusal arrives as a successful HTTP response, so transport-level retries never see it. Guidance is to read stop_details and retry on a fallback model, not to resend the same request in a loop. Anything still refused should surface for human review.
rationales: SDK retries cover connection errors, 429 and 5xx, not a 200 with a refusal.
Partial or refused output is not a valid extraction.
Correct. Distinct branch, bounded fallback, then review.
Refusal is not caused by the token limit.

sources.title: Handling stop reasons — Claude API docs

questions.scenario: Customer support agent with tools and escalation
questions.stem: After each tool call, the application sends the tool_result blocks followed by a text block: "Here are the results, please continue." Claude increasingly replies with stop_reason "end_turn" and almost no content. What is the most likely fix?
options: Retry the same request unchanged until a non-empty response appears
Stop adding text after the tool_result blocks and send only the tool results
Move the text block in front of the tool_result blocks
Raise max_tokens so the model has room to answer
questions.explanation: An empty end_turn after tool use is usually caused by adding text after the tool_result blocks. The fix is the message shape, not a retry. Putting text before the tool_result blocks is invalid and returns a 400.
rationales: Retrying unchanged is explicitly discouraged; the cause is still there.
tool_result blocks must come first; text before them is rejected.
The response was not truncated; it ended naturally with no content.

sources.title: Handle tool calls — Claude API docs

questions.stem: Which stop_reason values mean the model's output is truncated and must not be parsed as a finished answer? (Select two.)
options: max_tokens
end_turn
model_context_window_exceeded
stop_sequence
questions.explanation: max_tokens means the output hit your token limit, and model_context_window_exceeded means the context window filled. Both leave incomplete output. end_turn is a natural finish, and stop_sequence means one of your own stop sequences was produced.
rationales: Correct. Output hit the max_tokens limit.
Correct. The context window filled during generation.
