questions.scenario: Developer productivity tooling for a team
questions.stem: Every quarter, a compliance report must be built from the same five sections, each pulled from a known internal system, then merged into a fixed template. A team proposes an orchestrator agent that plans the subtasks for each run. What should the architect recommend?
options: Static decomposition: code the five subtasks (run in parallel where independent) and a fixed merge step with validation
Keep the orchestrator, because dynamic planning always finds better subtasks
A single autonomous agent with access to all five systems
Routing, so each quarter goes to a different specialist prompt
questions.explanation: The subtasks are known before the input arrives, which is the test for static decomposition. Coding them as fixed steps (sectioning plus a merge) is predictable, testable and cheaper. Dynamic planning only adds cost and variance here.
rationales: Dynamic planning is for subtasks that cannot be known in advance.
Adds unpredictability for a fixed process.
There are no distinct input categories to route between.

questions.stem: An engineer asks an agent to find why checkout latency regressed last week. The cause could be in any of a dozen services, and which ones matter depends on what the first traces show. Which decomposition fits best?
options: A fixed chain that inspects all twelve services in alphabetical order
Sectioning: run one predefined check per service in parallel and concatenate the output
Dynamic decomposition: an orchestrator plans initial investigations, delegates them, and revises the plan as findings come in, keeping the plan visible
A single call with all service logs pasted into the prompt
questions.explanation: The next steps depend on what earlier steps discover, so the subtasks cannot be listed in advance. That is the case for dynamic decomposition with a visible, revisable plan. Fixed chains or fixed parallel checks waste effort and cannot follow leads.
rationales: Ignores findings and spends effort on irrelevant services.
Predefined checks cannot adapt to what the traces reveal.
Floods the context and gives no way to dig deeper.

questions.stem: A research orchestrator plans search subtasks dynamically and works well, but sometimes skips citation checking or report formatting when it judges them unnecessary. Both must happen on every report. What is the best design?
options: Add "ALWAYS verify citations and format the report" to the orchestrator prompt
Lower max_turns so the orchestrator finishes faster and has time for formatting
Replace the orchestrator with a fixed chain for the whole task
Keep dynamic decomposition for the research phase, then run citation verification and formatting as fixed, coded stages after it
questions.explanation: A hybrid keeps model freedom where the path is genuinely unpredictable and puts must-always-happen steps in code. A prompt instruction stays probabilistic. Replacing everything with a fixed chain would lose the adaptive research the system needs.
rationales: Still probabilistic; the model can still skip the steps.
Turn caps do not ensure any particular step runs.
Loses dynamic planning where it is valuable.
Correct. Static stages guarantee the required steps.

questions.stem: A team's internal guide says Claude Code subagents cannot spawn their own subagents, so they flattened a review hierarchy. Which statement reflects current Claude Code behaviour?
options: Nesting is impossible; only the main conversation can spawn subagents
Subagents can nest without any limit
Nested subagents share the parent conversation's context window
Subagents can spawn subagents up to a configurable depth (3 layers by default), and nesting can be turned off
questions.explanation: Current Claude Code lets subagents spawn subagents, by default up to 3 layers below the main conversation, controlled by CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH (1 disables nesting). Each subagent still starts with its own fresh context. Older material that says nesting is impossible is out of date.
rationales: There is a default depth limit.
Each subagent gets a fresh context; only forks inherit.

questions.scenario: Developer productivity tooling for a team
questions.stem: After a long design discussion in Claude Code, a developer wants a side task to proceed with everything discussed so far, without restating it. Which choice gives the helper that context?
options: A normal subagent whose description says "use proactively"
A normal subagent with the tools field omitted
A normal subagent with model set to inherit
A fork, which inherits the parent conversation
questions.explanation: Normal subagents start with a fresh context and do not see the parent history. A fork is the documented exception and inherits the parent conversation. The other settings control tools, model choice and delegation, not context.
rationales: Affects when Claude delegates, not what context the subagent sees.
Omitting tools affects tool inheritance, not conversation context.
Model inheritance does not carry the conversation.

questions.stem: A "reviewer" subagent is defined with only name, description and a system prompt. During a review it posts a message through a Slack MCP tool. Why, and what is the fix?
options: MCP tools are never available to subagents, so the main conversation must have posted it
Its description lacks "use proactively", so it fell back to the general-purpose agent
With tools omitted it inherits all tools available to subagents, including MCP tools; set a tools allowlist (e.g. Read, Grep, Glob) or disallowedTools
Subagents always run with bypassPermissions, so add a permissionMode field
questions.explanation: Omitting tools means the subagent inherits every tool available to subagents, MCP tools included. Least privilege requires an explicit allowlist or denylist. A read-only reviewer has no need to post messages.
rationales: The description controls delegation, not tool access.
There is no such default; the issue is tool inheritance.

questions.scenario: Developer productivity tooling for a team
questions.stem: An Agent SDK job is configured with allowed_tools=["Read","Grep"] and permission_mode="acceptEdits". The team expected a read-only agent, but it edited files. What explains this, and what should they change?
options: A bug in the SDK; allowed_tools should hide every other tool
allowed_tools only auto-approves the listed tools, and acceptEdits approved the edits; block edit and shell tools with disallowed_tools and drop acceptEdits
Add "never edit files" to the system prompt
Lower max_turns so the agent has no turns left for editing
questions.explanation: allowed_tools auto-approves the listed tools but does not restrict the agent to them, and acceptEdits auto-approved the file edits. disallowed_tools blocks tools regardless of other settings. A prompt or a turn cap would not guarantee read-only behaviour.
rationales: This is documented behaviour, not a bug.
Probabilistic, and the configuration still allows edits.
Turn caps are not access control.

sources.title: Agent SDK overview — Claude Code docs

questions.stem: An Agent SDK run with max_budget_usd set to 5 ends with subtype "error_max_budget_usd" and total_cost_usd slightly above 5. How should the team read this?
options: It is a billing bug; the budget must never be exceeded
The budget is advisory and ignored by the SDK
The overshoot came from max_turns, not the budget
Expected: spend can overshoot by up to one response. Leave headroom and handle this subtype as an abnormal, partial outcome
questions.explanation: The budget cap can be overshot by up to one response, so it should be set with headroom. The error_max_budget_usd subtype shows the cap did trip. The run should be handled as a flagged partial outcome, not treated as success.
rationales: Documented behaviour allows a one-response overshoot.
The cap tripped, as the subtype shows.
The subtype names the budget, not turns.

questions.scenario: Developer productivity tooling for a team
questions.stem: A downstream job reads message.result from the final message of every Agent SDK run and occasionally crashes with a missing-field error. Which changes are correct? (Select two.)
options: Branch on the result message's subtype before reading result, because result is present only on success
Remove max_turns and max_budget_usd so runs always end in success
For error_max_turns and error_max_budget_usd, log total_cost_usd, num_turns and session_id, and surface a partial or resumable status
Use the last assistant text as the result for every subtype
questions.explanation: Only the success subtype carries result, so code must check subtype first. Limit subtypes are abnormal outcomes that should be logged with the metrics every result carries and surfaced as partial or resumable. Removing caps or passing off arbitrary text as the result hides failures.
rationales: Removes safety nets and still leaves error_during_execution.
Presents incomplete work as a finished result.

questions.stem: A nightly Agent SDK job runs with no human present. Any tool call that is not pre-approved should be denied rather than waiting for approval. Which permission mode fits?
options: bypassPermissions
plan
acceptEdits
dontAsk
questions.explanation: dontAsk auto-denies any call that would otherwise prompt, which suits unattended runs. bypassPermissions approves everything, acceptEdits auto-approves edits, and plan is a read-only planning mode, not a rule for denying calls that are not pre-approved.
rationales: Read-only planning; it is not the mode for auto-denying calls that would otherwise prompt.
Approves edits; it does not deny unapproved calls.

questions.scenario: Developer productivity tooling for a team
questions.stem: An organisation must guarantee that no developer's Claude Code session reads .env files. The platform team added the rule to the managed CLAUDE.md. What should they do instead?
options: Repeat the rule in each project CLAUDE.md in capital letters
Add a skill that explains why .env files are sensitive
Enforce it with a deny rule (e.g. Read(./.env)) in managed settings, optionally backed by a PreToolUse hook
Put the rule in a user-level ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md for each developer
questions.explanation: CLAUDE.md, including managed CLAUDE.md, is context, not enforcement. Managed settings such as permissions.deny cannot be overridden by users or projects, and a PreToolUse hook can block a call deterministically. More instructions in more places are still guidance.
rationales: Explains the rule but does not enforce it.
Still guidance, and developers control that file.

Every tool call must be written to the audit log
Prefer concise, friendly replies
Decide which knowledge-base article to read first
questions.explanation: Must-never and must-always requirements with real consequences belong in code, such as a PreToolUse hook or tool-side check, and a logging hook. Tone is a preference for the prompt. Choosing what to read is a judgment call the model should make.

Style guidance belongs in the prompt.

questions.scenario: Customer support agent with tools and escalation
questions.stem: A support agent's order tool calls an internal API that sometimes times out or returns 503, and sometimes returns 400 "invalid order id" when Claude passes a malformed id. Which handling is appropriate? (Select two.)
options: Retry timeouts and 503s with bounded exponential backoff before reporting failure
Return the 400 to Claude as a tool_result with is_error: true and an instructive message (expected id format) so it can correct the call
Retry every error five times with identical arguments
End the session on the first error of any kind
questions.explanation: Timeouts and 503s are transient, so bounded backoff is appropriate. A 400 for a malformed id is correctable: retrying it unchanged will fail again, but an instructive is_error result lets Claude fix the input. Treating all errors the same way either loops or gives up too early.
rationales: Correct. Correctable error fed back to the model.
Identical retries cannot fix an invalid input.

questions.stem: A coding agent has applied six "fixes" in a row, and each run produces the identical failing test output. It will keep going until max_turns trips. What should the design do instead?
options: Raise max_turns so the agent has more room to converge
Add "try harder and think carefully" to the system prompt
Let the agent delete or skip the failing test so the run goes green
Detect the lack of progress, switch to a different strategy (gather more information, smaller step), and if that fails, stop and report what was tried and what remains
questions.explanation: Repeating the same failure is a signal to change approach, not to continue. After an alternate strategy fails, the agent should stop and report with partial results so a human can decide. The turn cap is a backstop, not the plan.
rationales: More turns of the same loop waste budget.
Does not change the strategy or add a stopping rule.
Hides the failure and produces wrong code.

questions.stem: An automation receives 429 errors from the Claude API with no retry-after header. Investigation shows the organisation's spend cap was reached. The agent keeps retrying with backoff. What is the right behaviour?
options: Keep retrying with longer backoff; 429 is always transient
Treat it as persistent: stop the run, report or alert with context, and resume only after the cap is addressed
Switch to a different model and continue
Raise the SDK's max_retries to 20
questions.explanation: A spend-cap 429 has no retry-after header and keeps failing, so backoff cannot fix it. The right path is to classify it as persistent, stop, and surface it to someone who can act. More retries only add noise and delay.
rationales: Not every 429 is transient; this one will keep failing.
The cap applies to the organisation, not one model.
More retries of a persistent failure.

questions.scenario: Customer support agent with tools and escalation
questions.stem: An Agent SDK support agent can look up orders freely but must get a human's approval before each send_email call to a customer. What is the best mechanism?
options: Auto-approve the lookup tools with allowed_tools, and handle send_email in a canUseTool callback (or PreToolUse hook) that requests human approval and returns allow or deny
Run with bypassPermissions and tell the agent in the prompt to ask before emailing
Add send_email to disallowed_tools
Set max_turns to 1 so the agent cannot send email without a new run
questions.explanation: Read-only lookups can be auto-approved, while a high-impact action goes through a programmatic approval gate that a human answers. A prompt request offers no guarantee, and disallowing the tool removes the capability entirely. A turn cap is not an approval workflow.
rationales: Bypass removes every check; the prompt is not a gate.
Blocks email entirely instead of gating it.
Not an approval mechanism, and it breaks normal work.

questions.scenario: Developer productivity tooling for a team
questions.stem: A team wants every tool call an Agent SDK agent makes recorded in an audit log, without spending context tokens and without depending on the model to remember. What should they use?
options: A log_action tool the system prompt tells the agent to call after each action
A larger context window so the transcript can be kept and parsed later
Asking the agent to include a log summary in its final answer
A PostToolUse hook that writes each call and result to the log
questions.explanation: Hooks run deterministically in your own process and consume no context, so they suit must-always-happen logging. A logging tool depends on the model remembering to call it and costs tokens. A final summary is incomplete and unverifiable.
rationales: Does not create a structured, deterministic log.

questions.stem: A multi-hour Agent SDK run starts with a long first prompt containing house rules. After automatic compaction, the agent stops following some of those rules. What is the best fix?
options: Disable compaction so the original prompt is never summarised
Repeat the rules in capital letters at the start of the first prompt
Move the persistent rules into CLAUDE.md (with project settings loaded), which is re-injected after compaction
Lower max_turns so the run ends before compaction happens
questions.explanation: The SDK compacts automatically on long runs, and content from early turns can be summarised away. Persistent rules belong in CLAUDE.md, which is re-injected, rather than only in the initial prompt. Avoiding compaction or ending runs early just trades one failure for another.
rationales: Long runs would then exhaust the context window.
Still in the part of the conversation that gets compacted.

The project CLAUDE.md at the repo root (or .claude/CLAUDE.md), committed to version control

User-level configuration (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md and user settings), since they apply to that person across projects
The CI workflow file
A subdirectory CLAUDE.md

Create a separate repo for payments

Rename .env to .env.secret

A custom /format slash command

A skill describing formatting

questions.stem: A GitHub Actions step runs `claude "Fix lint errors in src/"` and the job hangs until timeout. What is wrong?
options: The model is too slow for CI
Without -p (print/headless mode), Claude Code starts an interactive session waiting for input. Use claude -p "..." with pre-authorized tools
GitHub Actions doesn't support Node.js
The prompt needs to be in JSON
questions.explanation: -p runs non-interactively, prints the result and exits, which is the required mode for scripts and CI.
rationales: Not the cause of an indefinite hang.

questions.stem: A pipeline needs to parse Claude Code's result (and metadata such as cost) programmatically. Which option helps most?
options: --output-format json
--verbose
Piping output through grep for "Result:"
Running interactively and copying the output
questions.explanation: JSON output (or stream-json) provides machine-readable results for automation.
rationales: Adds detail but isn't structured for parsing.

questions.stem: In CI, Claude Code should only read code and run the test command, nothing else. Which configuration choices are appropriate? (Select two.)
options: Pass --allowedTools limited to read/search tools and the specific test command (e.g. Bash(npm run test *))
Run with permissions fully bypassed on the shared CI runner that holds deploy secrets
Commit project settings with matching allow and deny rules so the policy is versioned and reviewed
Give the job an admin GitHub token so Claude never hits permission errors
questions.explanation: Least privilege in automation: pre-authorize exactly what's needed and version the policy. Bypass and admin tokens widen the blast radius.

questions.stem: A team asks the same Claude Code session that wrote a feature to review its own PR, and it approves everything. What should the architect recommend?
options: Ask the session to "be more critical"
Skip review because the code compiles
Increase the session's max turns
Run the review in an independent instance (separate CI job or a reviewer subagent with fresh context) against the requirements, plus deterministic checks
questions.explanation: Reviewing in the same context the code was written in reuses the assumptions that produced it. Recommended practice is an independent reviewer with fresh context (a separate instance or subagent) checking against the requirements, with deterministic checks such as tests and lint still deciding pass or fail.

questions.stem: A developer is about to ask Claude Code for a risky, cross-cutting refactor of unfamiliar code. Which workflow is recommended?
options: Ask for the full refactor immediately with auto-accept edits
Use plan mode to explore read-only and produce a plan, review and adjust it, then implement in steps with tests verifying each step
Disable tests to avoid noise
Do the refactor in one giant prompt with all files pasted in
questions.explanation: Explore, then plan, then implement, then verify, with plan mode for risky changes, gives a reviewable plan before edits.

A PreToolUse hook
A Skill (SKILL.md with a clear name/description, plus the template and script), which loads fully only when relevant
An MCP server that returns the procedure text
questions.explanation: Skills use progressive disclosure: the description stays in context and the full content loads when the task matches. They can bundle scripts and resources.
rationales: Hooks are for lifecycle automation, not procedures.
Heavier and not designed for this.

In the root CLAUDE.md
In a git-ignored .claude/settings.local.json
As .claude/skills/security-review/SKILL.md (with the checklist beside it), committed to the repo
questions.explanation: Custom slash commands are now skills: a committed project skill creates /security-review for everyone and can bundle supporting files. A legacy .claude/commands file would also work but cannot bundle the checklist as cleanly.
rationales: Personal scope; only the lead gets it.
Always-on memory, not an on-demand command, and it costs context every session.
Settings hold configuration, not commands, and this file is personal.

options: It can only be invoked from CI
It shares the main conversation's context window
It always has every tool available
It runs in its own context window with its own system prompt and can be restricted to specific tools
questions.explanation: Subagents provide context isolation and specialization, including restricted tool lists.
rationales: Tools can and should be restricted.

questions.stem: A shared project settings file allows Bash(git push *), but the organization's managed settings deny it. What happens when Claude tries to push?
options: Project settings win because they are more specific
The push is denied. Managed settings take precedence and deny rules beat allow rules
Claude asks the user to pick
The latest-edited file wins
questions.explanation: Deny rules are evaluated before allow rules and the first match wins, and managed settings cannot be loosened by lower scopes. The push is blocked.

questions.stem: A long Claude Code session has drifted across three unrelated tasks, and responses are getting worse. What is the best action before starting a fourth unrelated task?
options: Keep going. More context is always better
Restart the computer
Use /clear to start fresh (after saving anything important to CLAUDE.md or a notes file)
Paste the earlier conversation back in
questions.explanation: Irrelevant accumulated context degrades quality. Clear between unrelated tasks, and use /compact when you need to continue the same task with less context.

Split the guidance into path-scoped rules so only the relevant parts load for the files being worked on
Paste the whole document as the first message of every session
Put the document in each developer's personal settings.local.json

Run Claude Code interactively on a shared VM
Install the Claude GitHub app and anthropics/claude-code-action@v1 (e.g. via /install-github-app), then configure the workflow and API key secret

questions.stem: A team's CLAUDE.md has grown to 1,500 lines of mixed rules, history and notes. Claude increasingly ignores important instructions. What is the best remediation?

Bold every important line
Duplicate the most important rules three times
Move it into the system prompt of each request manually

A Stop hook that runs the tests and, on failure, blocks stopping and feeds the failures back to Claude
A slash command /tests
Set max-turns to a high value

options: Tell Claude to work faster
Delete the tests before asking
State explicitly that the tests define correct behaviour and must not be modified, and protect test files with deny rules or a hook if needed
Run the tests only at the end of the week

questions.stem: A developer must migrate an unfamiliar payments module from callbacks to async/await across 40 files. She wants to see and correct Claude's approach before any file changes. What should she do?
options: Switch to acceptEdits mode so the migration finishes faster, then review the diff
Start a subagent with all tools to do the migration in the background
Add "do not edit files until I say so" to CLAUDE.md
Enter plan mode (e.g. Shift+Tab or /plan), have Claude explore and propose a plan, revise it, then approve and implement in verified steps
questions.explanation: Plan mode keeps Claude read-only until the plan is approved, which gives a review checkpoint before edits on risky, unfamiliar work. Implementing in steps with tests afterwards keeps each change verifiable.
rationales: Removes the review point entirely; reviewing 40 changed files after the fact is the costly path.

questions.stem: Which task gains the least from starting in plan mode?
options: Splitting a 3,000-line module into packages
Redesigning the authentication flow in a service the developer has never seen
Changing a database schema that several services depend on
Renaming a misspelled local variable in one function the developer just wrote
questions.explanation: Plan mode pays off when the approach is uncertain or the blast radius is wide. For a tiny, well-understood edit, the diff is the plan, and a planning round only adds overhead.
rationales: Large structural change: a plan exposes ordering and dependency issues.
Unfamiliar code and high risk: plan first.
Cross-service impact: plan the order and rollback first.
Correct: small, local and well understood.

sources.title: Permission modes (plan mode) — Claude Code docs

questions.stem: A team lead says: "We run every session on the untrusted vendor repo in plan mode, so Claude can never touch our secrets." What is the best response?
options: Correct, plan mode is a sandbox that blocks all reads outside the repo
Correct, as long as CLAUDE.md also forbids reading secrets
Plan mode is a review checkpoint, not a security boundary: Claude can still read files. Protect secrets with deny rules (e.g. Read(./.env)), managed settings and the sandbox
Switch to bypassPermissions so nothing prompts the user during review
questions.explanation: Plan mode stops edits until a plan is approved, but Claude still reads and explores. Hard guarantees come from permission deny rules, managed policy and OS-level sandboxing.
rationales: Plan mode is read-only, which still allows reading secrets.

sources.title: Permission modes (plan mode) — Claude Code docs

questions.scenario: Developer productivity tooling for a team
questions.stem: A platform team wants every new Claude Code session in a legacy monolith to start read-only and produce a plan before editing, without each developer remembering to switch modes. What should they configure?
options: Set "defaultMode": "plan" under permissions in the committed .claude/settings.json
Add a SessionStart hook that prints "please plan first"
Add a line to CLAUDE.md asking Claude to plan first
Deny the Edit and Write tools permanently in managed settings

rationales: Only adds context; it does not change the mode.
Probabilistic guidance, not a mode change.
Blocks implementation entirely, even after a plan is approved.

questions.stem: The root CLAUDE.md says "use npm" and packages/web/CLAUDE.md says "use pnpm". Running Claude from packages/web, it sometimes picks npm. What explains this, and what is the fix?
options: The nearest file overrides the root, so this is a model bug; report it
Both files are concatenated into context, so Claude sees contradictory instructions; remove the conflict, e.g. state the per-package rule once in the root or drop the root rule
Subdirectory files are ignored unless imported with @
CLAUDE.local.md always overrides both; put the rule there
questions.explanation: CLAUDE.md files from the root down to the working directory are concatenated, not overridden, so both instructions reach the model. Contradictions must be fixed in the files themselves.
rationales: There is no override; both load.
Files on the path to the cwd load at launch; subtree files load on demand.
CLAUDE.local.md is appended, not an override, and it is personal.

~/.claude/CLAUDE.md

.claude/rules/sandbox.md

questions.stem: To "save tokens", a team splits its 600-line CLAUDE.md into ten files and @imports all of them from CLAUDE.md. Context usage is unchanged. Why, and what would actually help?
options: They should import with absolute paths, which are cached
Imports only work up to one level deep, so the files are not loading at all
The files must be JSON to be compressed
Imports load the same content, so cost is unchanged; move area-specific guidance into path-scoped rules or subdirectory CLAUDE.md files, and procedures into skills
questions.explanation: Imports organize memory but are loaded at launch like inline text. Content only stops costing context when it loads conditionally (path rules, subtree files) or on invocation (skills).

questions.stem: A team writes .claude/rules/migrations.md with database migration conventions, but the rule appears in every session, even docs-only work. What change makes it load only when Claude works on migration files?
options: Rename it to migrations.local.md
Add `@db/migrations` at the top of the rule
Move it into ~/.claude/rules/
Add YAML frontmatter with `paths:` globs, e.g. `- "db/migrations/**/*.sql"`

That is import syntax, not path scoping.
Changes the scope to personal, still unconditional.

questions.stem: Project settings contain `"deny": ["Bash(git push *)"]`. A developer adds `"allow": ["Bash(git push origin feature/*)"]` to settings.local.json, expecting the more specific rule to win. What happens?
options: The push is allowed: local settings have higher precedence than project settings
The push is allowed: more specific rules win
The push is denied: deny rules are evaluated first and the first match wins, regardless of specificity
Claude asks which rule to apply
questions.explanation: Permission rules are evaluated deny, then ask, then allow, and array settings merge across scopes. The project deny matches first, so the more specific local allow never applies.
rationales: Local settings rank above project settings, but permission arrays merge across scopes and deny is still evaluated first.
Specificity does not change the evaluation order.
Rules are deterministic; there is no tie-break prompt.

questions.scenario: Developer productivity tooling for a team
questions.stem: A contributor's PR sets `"defaultMode": "bypassPermissions"` in the repo's committed .claude/settings.json. What is true? (Select two.)
options: bypassPermissions does not take effect from project or local settings files
Every teammate who pulls the change will now run with all prompts skipped
Admins can disable bypass mode org-wide with permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode: "disable" in managed settings
The setting takes effect for each developer once they accept the workspace trust prompt
questions.explanation: Claude Code ignores the auto and bypassPermissions default modes when they come from project or local files, so a committed file cannot silently loosen everyone's permissions. Organizations can also disable bypass mode entirely via managed settings.
rationales: Wrong: the mode is not honoured from project files.
Trust gates project allow rules, but bypassPermissions is never honoured from project files.

questions.stem: A team wants Claude to run tests freely, always confirm before `git push`, and never read files under secrets/. Which settings.json fragment matches?
options: `allow: ["Bash(npm run test *)", "Bash(git push *)"], deny: ["Read(./secrets/**)"]`
`allow: ["Bash(*)"], deny: ["Read(./secrets/**)", "Bash(git push *)"]`
`ask: ["Bash(npm run test *)"], allow: ["Bash(git push *)"], deny: ["Read(./secrets/**)"]`
`allow: ["Bash(npm run test *)"], ask: ["Bash(git push *)"], deny: ["Read(./secrets/**)"]`
questions.explanation: allow pre-approves, ask forces a confirmation, and deny blocks. Tests go in allow, pushes in ask, and secret reads in deny.
rationales: Pushes would run with no confirmation.
Blocks pushes entirely and over-allows all shell commands.
Prompts for tests and auto-approves pushes: inverted.

questions.stem: A PreToolUse hook script detects `rm -rf` in a Bash command, prints a reason to stderr and exits with code 1. The command still runs. What is the fix?
options: Exit with code 2 (or return permissionDecision "deny" in JSON), which blocks the call and feeds the reason back to Claude
Print the reason to stdout instead
Move the hook to PostToolUse
Add "never run rm -rf" to CLAUDE.md as a backup
questions.explanation: Only exit code 2 is blocking for hook events like PreToolUse; other non-zero codes, including 1, are non-blocking errors. A JSON permissionDecision of "deny" is the structured alternative.
rationales: With exit 1 the call is still not blocked.
PostToolUse runs after the command already executed.
Guidance only; it does not repair the hook.

questions.scenario: Developer productivity tooling for a team
questions.stem: A developer wants Claude to investigate a flaky test by reading many large log files, without filling the main session's context. Which extension point fits best?
options: A PostToolUse hook
A line in CLAUDE.md
A subagent with read-only tools that returns a short summary to the main session
An entry in .mcp.json
questions.explanation: Subagents start with a fresh context and only their summary returns to the parent, which suits noisy, isolated investigation. Hooks are for deterministic lifecycle actions and CLAUDE.md for always-on facts.
rationales: Hooks automate fixed actions; they do not investigate.
Always-on memory does not isolate context.
Adds an MCP server, not context isolation.

questions.scenario: Developer productivity tooling for a team
questions.stem: A team has a `/deploy-staging` procedure with side effects. They want it available to everyone as a slash command but never triggered by Claude on its own initiative. What should they build?
options: A subagent named deploy-staging with "use proactively" in its description
A project skill at .claude/skills/deploy-staging/SKILL.md with `disable-model-invocation: true`, committed to the repo
A CLAUDE.md section describing the deploy steps
A Stop hook that deploys whenever Claude finishes a turn
questions.explanation: Skills create slash commands, and `disable-model-invocation` keeps a procedure user-triggered only. Committing it under .claude/skills shares it with the team.
rationales: "Use proactively" encourages automatic delegation: the opposite of what is wanted.
Always-on context that Claude may act on without an explicit command.
Deploys on every turn: dangerous and not on demand.

questions.stem: After upgrading Claude Code, a nightly `claude -p "update the changelog"` job finishes but makes no edits, and the log shows denied Edit calls. Nothing else changed. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: CLAUDE.md is missing, so Claude refuses to edit
The model got worse at writing; switch models
The job needs --verbose to enable edits
Headless runs now start in Manual mode, so calls needing approval are denied; pre-approve the needed tools (e.g. --allowedTools "Read,Edit") or use --permission-mode acceptEdits
questions.explanation: Current versions start `-p` in Manual mode and deny any call that would need approval unless a rule, flag or mode approves it. The job must explicitly authorize what it needs.
rationales: CLAUDE.md is guidance; its absence does not block tools.
The log shows permission denials, not quality problems.

questions.stem: A CI job runs Claude Code on pull requests from external forks. A reviewer notices the fork's .claude/settings.json defines hooks and its .mcp.json adds a server. Which measures reduce the risk? (Select two.)
options: Run with --bare so project hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers and CLAUDE.md from the fork are skipped
Rely on the workspace trust prompt to stop untrusted hooks
Give the job a least-privilege token and a restricted --allowedTools list
Add a CLAUDE.md line telling Claude to ignore the fork's hooks
questions.explanation: Without --bare, `-p` runs project hooks and .mcp.json servers even in an untrusted folder with no trust prompt. --bare removes that attack surface, and least privilege limits the damage if something still goes wrong.
rationales: Headless runs show no trust prompt.
Hooks run outside the model; instructions cannot stop them, and the fork controls CLAUDE.md anyway.

questions.stem: A pipeline needs Claude Code to return `{"severity": ..., "files": [...]}` that a later step consumes. Which approach is most reliable?
options: Ask for JSON in the prompt and parse the text with a regex
Use --output-format text and pipe it through jq
Run claude -p with --output-format json and --json-schema, read structured_output, and fail the step if it is missing
Run interactively and copy the JSON by hand
questions.explanation: --json-schema with JSON output validates against the schema and puts the data in structured_output. That field is absent when no valid output was produced, so the pipeline must check for it.
rationales: Text output is not JSON; jq would fail.

questions.stem: A team migrating from the beta GitHub Action has `direct_prompt: "Review this PR"` and a separate `max_turns: 5` input. How should the workflow look with anthropics/claude-code-action@v1?
options: Keep direct_prompt and max_turns unchanged
Use `prompt: "Review this PR"` and pass CLI options through `claude_args: "--max-turns 5"`
Put the prompt in CLAUDE.md and delete the inputs
Use `direct_prompt` with `claude_args` and drop prompt
questions.explanation: In v1, `direct_prompt` became `prompt`, and CLI options moved into `claude_args`. Turn limits, models and allowed tools are passed there.
rationales: CLAUDE.md is memory, not the automation prompt.
direct_prompt is the old input name.

questions.stem: A scheduled Claude Code job occasionally loops on a hard task and runs up large bills. Which controls cap it? (Select two.)
options: --max-turns and --max-budget-usd on the claude -p call (or in claude_args)
A workflow-level timeout and concurrency limit on the CI job
A CLAUDE.md line asking Claude to be economical
--verbose so the loop is easier to see
questions.explanation: Turn and budget limits stop the agent itself, while CI timeouts and concurrency limits bound the job around it. Instructions and logging do not cap spend.

questions.scenario: Developer productivity tooling for a team
questions.stem: A team wants every developer to get the same GitHub MCP server, the same permission rules and the same reviewer subagent when they clone the repo, without committing secrets. What should they commit?
options: .claude/settings.local.json and each developer's ~/.claude.json
.mcp.json (token referenced as ${GITHUB_TOKEN}), .claude/settings.json and .claude/agents/reviewer.md
A README telling everyone how to run claude mcp add locally
.mcp.json with the token pasted inline, plus CLAUDE.local.md
questions.explanation: Project-scope MCP servers live in a committed .mcp.json with environment-variable expansion for secrets, team permissions in .claude/settings.json, and shared subagents in .claude/agents/. Local files and ~/.claude.json are personal.
rationales: Manual and drifts; local-scope servers are not shared.
Commits a secret, and CLAUDE.local.md is personal.

questions.scenario: Customer support agent with tools and escalation
questions.stem: A support system prompt has grown to 120 special-case IF-THEN rules. Each fix for one case breaks another. What is the best approach?
options: Add more rules with higher priority labels
Restate the underlying principles and goals with reasons, add a few diverse examples, route very different request types to separate prompts, and validate with an eval set
Remove the system prompt entirely
Translate the rules into a single paragraph
questions.explanation: Principles plus examples generalize better than ever-growing conditionals, which conflict and dilute. Routing splits truly different tasks, and evals catch regressions.

sources.title: Prompting best practices — Claude API docs

questions.stem: A prompt contains instructions, a contract and example outputs mixed together, and Claude sometimes treats contract text as instructions. What helps most?
options: Write everything in capital letters
Use a higher temperature
Shorten the contract by removing pages
Wrap each part in distinct XML tags such as <instructions>, <contract> and <examples>, and refer to them by name
questions.explanation: XML tags clearly separate instructions from data, which reduces confusion and makes prompts easier to maintain.

sources.title: Prompting best practices — Claude API docs

questions.stem: An extraction pipeline runs on a current Claude model. Which approach most reliably yields JSON that parses and conforms to the target schema?
options: Structured outputs (output_config.format with a JSON schema) or a tool defined with strict: true, followed by validation in code
Asking "respond only in JSON" at the end of the prompt
Regex-extracting the first { ... } block from prose
Asking the model to double-check its JSON
questions.explanation: Structured outputs and strict tools use constrained decoding, so the output conforms to the schema. Code validation then adds the business-rule and range checks the schema can't express.
rationales: Works often, but gives no guarantee.
Fragile and breaks on nested braces or prose.

questions.stem: Extracted invoices pass JSON schema validation but sometimes have totals that don't match their line items. What should the pipeline add?
options: Nothing. Schema validation is sufficient
A stronger instruction to "be accurate"
Business-rule validation in code (sum of line items equals total) with a bounded retry that feeds back the specific discrepancy, then human review if it persists
Drop line items from the schema
questions.explanation: Schema conformance isn't correctness. Semantic checks plus targeted feedback retries plus escalation make extraction reliable.

sources.title: Handle tool calls — Claude API docs

questions.stem: After a validation failure, the pipeline resends the identical request, and it fails the same way 3 times. What is the better retry?
options: Retry 10 more times
Increase temperature to 1.0 and retry
Switch to free-text output
Retry with the original input plus the specific validation errors (e.g. "due_date '31/02/2026' is not a valid date"), bounded, then escalate
questions.explanation: Feedback-driven retries give the model the information needed to correct itself, and bounding prevents loops.

sources.title: Handle tool calls — Claude API docs

questions.scenario: Customer support agent with tools and escalation
questions.stem: A classifier routes tickets into five categories. Accuracy is poor on edge cases. What is the most effective prompt improvement?
options: Remove the category definitions to reduce tokens
Add one example and repeat it three times
Ask for the answer in uppercase
Add 3–5 diverse, representative examples (including tricky edge cases) in <example> tags, define each category clearly, and include an "other" category
questions.explanation: Diverse few-shot examples are one of the most powerful steering tools. Clear definitions and an escape category prevent forced misclassification.

sources.title: Prompting best practices — Claude API docs

questions.stem: A complex analysis task on Claude Opus 5.5 has errors in intermediate reasoning. The output must remain a clean, parseable answer. What is the best technique?
options: Forbid any reasoning so the answer is shorter
Rely on adaptive thinking at a higher effort level and return the result through structured outputs, so the thinking stays out of the parsed answer
Instruct the model to write its full step-by-step reasoning in <thinking> tags before an <answer> block
Set thinking to {type: "enabled"} with a large budget_tokens
questions.explanation: On current models, reasoning comes from built-in thinking, and the effort level controls how much it does. Structured outputs keep the final answer parseable. Asking for visible reasoning can trigger reasoning_extraction refusals, and manual thinking is removed on 4.7+ models.
rationales: Hurts accuracy on complex tasks, and thinking can't be disabled on Opus 5.5 anyway.
Classic CoT is a fallback for models without thinking. On the newest models it can trigger a reasoning_extraction refusal.
Manual extended thinking returns a 400 on Claude 4.7+ models.

sources.title: Prompting best practices — Claude API docs

questions.stem: A team relies on prefilling the assistant turn with "{" to force JSON. They plan to move to Claude Sonnet 5.5. What should the architect advise?
options: Prefill works on every model, so no change is needed
Add two opening braces for extra reliability
Prefill is unsupported on Claude 4.6+ models and returns a 400. Migrate to structured outputs (or strict tools) with a schema
Disable JSON and parse prose
questions.explanation: Assistant-message prefill is rejected on Claude 4.6+ models. Structured outputs give a stronger guarantee than prefill ever did.
rationales: Less reliable and harder to validate.

sources.title: Prompting best practices — Claude API docs

questions.scenario: Customer support agent with tools and escalation
questions.stem: What belongs in the system prompt versus the user turn for a support assistant?
options: Everything goes in the user turn, and the system prompt is unused
The customer's question goes in the system prompt
The system prompt is only for the model name
The system prompt holds role, standing context, policies and tone. The user turn holds the specific customer request and task data
questions.explanation: The system prompt sets persistent role and context, and per-request content goes in the messages.
rationales: Leaves no place for stable role and policy, so they get repeated or lost per request.
The system prompt carries role, policies and tone; the model name is a request parameter, not prompt content.

sources.title: Prompting best practices — Claude API docs

questions.scenario: Customer support agent with tools and escalation
questions.stem: An instruction says "Never use ellipses." A teammate suggests rewriting it as "Your response will be read aloud by a text-to-speech engine, so never use ellipses, since the engine can't pronounce them." Why is the rewrite better?
options: Explaining the reason helps Claude generalize to related cases (e.g. avoiding other unpronounceable symbols)
Longer prompts are always better
It disables the model's creativity
It forces deterministic output
questions.explanation: Context and motivation behind instructions improve adherence and generalization.

sources.title: Prompting best practices — Claude API docs

questions.stem: In an extraction schema, the field "document_type" must be one of invoice, receipt or credit_note, but the model sometimes outputs "bill". What is the best schema change?
options: Add a post-processing regex
Make document_type an enum of the allowed values plus "other", with a separate free-text detail field for unexpected types
Allow any string
Remove the field
questions.explanation: Enums constrain closed sets, and an escape value with a detail field avoids forcing wrong classifications.
rationales: Patches symptoms after the fact; the schema still allows invalid values.

questions.stem: Which techniques reduce hallucinated values in structured extraction? (Select three.)
options: Nullable fields with an explicit instruction to use null when a value isn't present
Requiring a source_quote field for key extracted values
Making every field required with no null allowed
Validating extracted values against source data or business rules in code
questions.explanation: Allowing absence, requiring grounding quotes and validating in code all reduce fabrication. Required-everything increases it.

questions.scenario: Developer productivity tooling for a team
questions.stem: A team changes a production prompt weekly by editing it in a dashboard, with no record. Regressions keep surprising them. What practice fixes this?
options: Freeze the prompt forever
Let the model rewrite its own prompt
Change prompts only on Fridays
Version prompts like code (in git with review) and run an eval suite on every change before deploying
questions.explanation: Prompt versioning plus evals give traceability and catch regressions before production.

sources.title: Prompt engineering overview — Claude API docs

questions.stem: Claude's output style is too terse and bullet-heavy for a report that should be flowing prose. Which instruction style works best?
options: "Don't use bullets. Don't be terse. Don't use markdown."
"Write the report in flowing prose paragraphs, written for executives, with smooth transitions between ideas."
"Be better."
Raise temperature
questions.explanation: Telling Claude what to do (positive framing) with context works better than a list of prohibitions.

sources.title: Prompting best practices — Claude API docs

questions.stem: A complex contract analysis prompt does clause extraction, risk scoring and summary in one call, and errors are hard to localize. What is the better design?
options: Shorten the contract
Add more instructions to the single prompt
Use three models in parallel on the full task and vote
A prompt chain: extract clauses (validated), then score risk on the extracted clauses, then summarize. Each step is focused and inspectable
questions.explanation: Chaining separates concerns. You can validate intermediate outputs and retry only the failing step.

sources.title: Prompting best practices — Claude API docs

questions.scenario: Customer support agent with tools and escalation
questions.stem: All five few-shot examples in a sentiment prompt have short inputs labelled "positive". In production the model over-predicts positive and struggles with long reviews. What is the issue?
options: Few-shot examples never help
The model needs a lower temperature
The examples share accidental patterns (length, label), which the model copies. Use diverse examples across labels and lengths, including edge cases
There are too many examples
questions.explanation: Models pick up on patterns in examples, including unintended ones. Diversity matters.

sources.title: Prompting best practices — Claude API docs

questions.stem: Where should field-specific extraction guidance, such as "amount in minor units (cents) as integer", be placed when using a tool schema for extraction?
options: Only in a separate README
In the tool name
Nowhere. The model infers it
In the property's description inside the input_schema (and optionally reinforced in the prompt)
questions.explanation: Schema property descriptions act as instructions where the model needs them.
rationales: Without stated guidance the model may use dollars, strings or cents inconsistently.

questions.stem: You need to extract data from 500,000 archived documents by next week. Latency per document doesn't matter. Which approach is most cost-effective?
options: Synchronous calls with maximum concurrency
Use the Message Batches API for asynchronous processing at lower cost, with schema validation on results
Process them manually
Use the largest model with extended thinking on every document
questions.explanation: Batch processing suits large, non-urgent workloads and is significantly cheaper.

questions.scenario: Customer support agent with tools and escalation
questions.stem: Which practices make a production system prompt more robust? (Select two.)
options: Clear role and goals with reasons, plus concise examples of desired behaviour
Hundreds of narrow special-case rules accumulated from incident fixes
An eval suite run on each prompt change
Contradictory instructions so the model can choose
questions.explanation: Principled, example-backed prompts plus systematic evaluation are robust. Rule sprawl and contradictions aren't.

sources.title: Prompting best practices — Claude API docs
Prompt engineering overview — Claude API docs

questions.stem: Briefing Claude for a task, which description best reflects good prompting?
options: Assume Claude knows your company's internal conventions
Keep instructions vague to allow creativity
Write it like a brief for a brilliant new colleague with no context: the goal, audience, constraints, output format and what success looks like
Only provide the output format
questions.explanation: Clear, direct and context-rich prompts consistently produce better results.
rationales: It doesn't know them unless told.

sources.title: Prompting best practices — Claude API docs

questions.stem: After moving a research agent from an older model to Claude Opus 5.5, every request fails with a 400. The request sets thinking: {type: "enabled", budget_tokens: 8000}. What is the best fix?
options: Lower budget_tokens to 2000
Switch to thinking: {type: "adaptive"} and set output_config.effort to the level the task needs
Remove the thinking parameter and tell the model to reason step by step in <thinking> tags
Set thinking: {type: "disabled"} to restore the old behaviour
questions.explanation: Manual extended thinking was removed on Claude 4.7+ models, so type "enabled" is rejected whatever the budget. Adaptive thinking with an effort level is the replacement.
rationales: The 400 comes from type "enabled" itself, not the budget size.
Asking the newest models to write visible reasoning can trigger reasoning_extraction refusals, and it drops the supported adaptive thinking control instead of fixing the request.
Thinking can't be disabled on Opus 5.5.

sources.title: Prompting best practices — Claude API docs

questions.stem: A claims-triage service on Claude Sonnet 5.5 uses structured outputs with a schema that includes a required "reasoning" string where the model must explain its decision step by step. Some requests now come back as refusals citing reasoning_extraction. Reviewers still want a rationale. What should the architect change?
options: Retry refused requests unchanged until they succeed
Move the step-by-step reasoning request into the system prompt marked CRITICAL
Replace the "reasoning" field with a short "explanation" field and rely on the model's built-in thinking, adjusting effort if accuracy needs it
Remove structured outputs and parse the reasoning out of free text
questions.explanation: On the newest models, asking for step-by-step reasoning in the output or a schema field can trigger a reasoning_extraction refusal. A brief explanation meets the reviewers' need while the reasoning happens in built-in thinking.
rationales: The same request will tend to be refused again.
Still requests extracted reasoning, and aggressive wording overtriggers.
Loses schema guarantees and still requests visible reasoning.

sources.title: Prompting best practices — Claude API docs

questions.scenario: Customer support agent with tools and escalation
questions.stem: A high-volume intent classifier runs on Claude Opus 5.5. Accuracy is fine, but latency and cost are too high for such a simple task. Which change fits the model's controls?
options: Set thinking: {type: "disabled"}
Lower output_config.effort for this workload and confirm accuracy holds on the eval set
Set a small manual budget_tokens
Add "do not think" to the system prompt
questions.explanation: Thinking can't be disabled on Opus 5.5, and manual budgets are rejected on 4.7+ models. Effort is the lever for trading reasoning for speed, and the eval set confirms nothing regressed.
rationales: Manual extended thinking returns a 400 on Claude 4.7+.
Prompt text doesn't control the thinking budget reliably.

sources.title: Prompting best practices — Claude API docs

questions.stem: A team needs better reasoning on a hard multi-step financial analysis using Claude Opus 5.5. Which approaches are appropriate? (Select two.)
options: Use adaptive thinking with a higher output_config.effort
Split the work into draft, review and refine calls so each intermediate output can be inspected and validated
Require the full step-by-step reasoning in the visible output inside <thinking> tags
Enable manual extended thinking with a large budget_tokens
questions.explanation: Built-in adaptive thinking at higher effort and explicit self-correction chains both improve hard reasoning on current models. Visible-reasoning prompts risk reasoning_extraction refusals, and manual thinking is removed on 4.7+.
rationales: May trigger a reasoning_extraction refusal on the newest models.

sources.title: Prompting best practices — Claude API docs

questions.stem: A team passes an invoice schema through output_config.format. The top-level object sets additionalProperties: false, but the nested "vendor" and "line_item" objects don't, and the API rejects the schema. What is the fix?
options: Switch back to the deprecated output_format parameter
Remove the nested objects and flatten everything into strings
Add additionalProperties: false to every object in the schema, including nested ones
Prefill the response with "{" instead
questions.explanation: Structured outputs require additionalProperties: false on every object, not just the root. Fixing the schema keeps the constrained-decoding guarantee.
rationales: Deprecated, and it doesn't remove the schema requirement.
Loses useful structure; the real problem is the missing flag.
Prefill is unsupported on Claude 4.6+ models.

questions.stem: An extraction service uses structured outputs. A developer proposes deleting all response checks because constrained decoding guarantees the schema. Which checks should stay in code? (Select two.)
options: Check stop_reason, because a refusal or max_tokens stop can produce output that doesn't conform
Validate value ranges and business rules, such as totals matching line items, which the schema can't express
Repair mismatched brackets in every successful response
Sort the keys of every object into schema order
questions.explanation: Constrained decoding guarantees structure on a normal completion only, and schemas can't express numeric ranges or cross-field rules. Bracket repair and key sorting address problems that conforming output doesn't have.
rationales: Unnecessary on conforming output; check stop_reason instead.
JSON key order isn't a correctness issue.

sources.title: Handling stop reasons — Claude API docs

questions.stem: An extractor that uses tool_choice: {type: "tool", name: "record_invoice"} is moved to Claude Sonnet 5.5, and requests now fail with a 400 about tool_choice. What is the best replacement?
options: Use tool_choice {type: "any"} with only record_invoice defined
Prefill the assistant turn with the start of the tool call
Use structured outputs with the invoice schema, or keep the tool with strict: true under tool_choice auto
Drop tools and ask for JSON in the prompt
questions.explanation: Forced tool use ("tool" and "any") isn't supported on the newest flagship models. Structured outputs or strict tools give schema conformance without forcing.
rationales: "any" is rejected on the same models.
Prefill is unsupported on Claude 4.6+ models.
Works sometimes but gives no schema guarantee.

questions.scenario: Customer support agent with tools and escalation
questions.stem: A support assistant's system prompt template starts with "Today is {date}. You are helping {customer_name} with: {question}" followed by 6,000 tokens of policy. Cache hits are zero and the template is hard to review. What is the best restructuring?
options: Keep the stable role and policy in the system prompt, and send the date, customer name and question in the user message after it
Move the policy into the user message and leave the system prompt empty
Put the date at the end of the system prompt but keep the question at the top
Shorten the policy to a single sentence
questions.explanation: Stable instructions belong in the system prompt, which forms a cacheable prefix. Per-request values belong in the messages. Variable text at the top of the system prompt changes the prefix on every call.
rationales: Loses the system prompt's role, and the policy would still sit behind changing content.
The question at the top still breaks the prefix.

questions.stem: A legal assistant answers questions about a 90-page contract plus two amendments. Answers often miss relevant clauses. Which prompt layout is best?
options: State the question first, then paste the contract and amendments as one block

Put the three documents at the top in <documents> with an indexed <document> per file (with <source> and <document_content>), ask for relevant quotes in <quotes> tags, and place the question at the end
Put the question in capital letters before and after the documents
Summarize the contract first in a separate call and discard the original
questions.explanation: Long documents go at the top with the query at the end, and indexed document tags help Claude tell sources apart. Extracting quotes first grounds the answer in the text.
rationales: Query-first ordering with an untagged blob performs worse.
Emphasis doesn't fix ordering or structure.
Discarding the source loses detail needed for clause-level answers.

sources.title: Prompting best practices — Claude API docs

questions.scenario: Customer support agent with tools and escalation
questions.stem: After an upgrade to a newer Claude model, an agent whose prompt says "CRITICAL: You MUST ALWAYS call search_kb before answering" now calls search_kb even for greetings and thank-you messages. What is the best fix?
options: Add "CRITICAL: NEVER call search_kb for greetings"
Remove the search_kb tool
Rewrite the instruction calmly with its purpose, e.g. "Use search_kb when a question depends on product or policy details, so answers match current documentation"
Raise the temperature
questions.explanation: Newer models follow instructions closely, so aggressive wording overtriggers. Plain wording that explains when and why lets the model generalize.
rationales: Piles on more aggressive, conflicting rules.

sources.title: Prompting best practices — Claude API docs

questions.scenario: Developer productivity tooling for a team
questions.stem: A team will change a production extraction prompt and move to a newer model in the same release. Which practices best catch regressions before customers do? (Select two.)
options: Keep prompt versions in version control with review, and log which version served each request
Run the old and new configurations on the same representative eval set with edge cases and code-graded checks, and compare against the baseline
Ask the new model to judge whether its own outputs improved, with no rubric
Deploy to all traffic and roll back if complaints rise
questions.explanation: Versioning gives traceability, and a regression eval on a fixed set gives a measurable comparison before release. Unstructured self-judgment and production-as-test catch problems late or not at all.

sources.title: Prompt engineering overview — Claude API docs

questions.scenario: Customer support agent with tools and escalation
questions.stem: An order agent calls create_order with quantity: -3. Your code's validation rejects it. What should the agent loop send back?
options: A new user message saying "Try again" with no detail
A success result with quantity silently changed to 1
Nothing; end the conversation
A tool_result with is_error: true and a specific message such as "quantity must be a positive integer; got -3"
questions.explanation: Returning the error as a tool_result with is_error: true and specific text lets Claude correct the input and retry. Silent fixes and vague retries hide the problem or waste turns.
rationales: Gives Claude nothing to correct from, and breaks the tool_use/tool_result pairing.
Records data the user never asked for.

sources.title: Handle tool calls — Claude API docs

questions.scenario: Customer support agent with tools and escalation
questions.stem: An agent has search_orders, find_order and lookup_order_by_id tools with one-line descriptions, and frequently picks the wrong one. What is the best fix?
options: Add a fourth tool, get_order, with a clearer name
Consolidate the overlapping tools into one task-shaped tool with a detailed description (purpose, when to use, parameter formats, return values)
Lower temperature so tool selection is deterministic
Use tool_choice "any" so the model must call a tool
questions.explanation: Overlapping tools with terse descriptions confuse selection. Fewer, distinct, well-described tools are the main lever.
rationales: Forces a call but not the right one.

sources.title: Writing tools for agents — Anthropic Engineering

questions.stem: An extraction service on Sonnet 5.5 defines a record_invoice tool and sets tool_choice to {"type": "tool", "name": "record_invoice"} so output always matches the schema. Every request now fails with a 400 error about tool_choice. What is the best fix?
options: Switch tool_choice to {"type": "any"} so some tool is still forced
Use structured outputs (output_config.format) with the invoice schema, or keep the tool with tool_choice auto and strict: true
Remove the tool and prefill the assistant turn with "{" to start JSON
Retry the request with exponential backoff until it succeeds
questions.explanation: Forced tool use (tool_choice any or tool) is not supported on the newest models such as Sonnet 5.5 and returns 400. Structured outputs, or a strict tool under auto, give schema-conforming output on those models. Prefill is also unsupported on current models.
rationales: any is forced tool use too, so it fails the same way.
Prefill is rejected on current models.
A 400 is a permanent request error; retrying will not help.

questions.scenario: Customer support agent with tools and escalation
questions.stem: The get_customer tool fails because the ID doesn't exist. The current handler returns an empty string, and the agent then tells customers "you have no account". What should the handler return?
options: A tool_result with is_error: true and an actionable message, e.g. "NOT_FOUND: no customer with id C-991. Ask the user to confirm their email or ID."
Raise an exception to terminate the agent loop
Return a fake default customer record so the flow continues
Return the HTTP status code number only
questions.explanation: Structured, actionable errors let the model recover correctly. Empty strings are ambiguous and exceptions kill the loop on an expected condition.

sources.title: Handle tool calls — Claude API docs
Writing tools for agents — Anthropic Engineering

questions.scenario: Customer support agent with tools and escalation
questions.stem: The charge_card tool timed out. You don't know whether the charge succeeded. What is the safest design?
options: Retry immediately. Timeouts usually mean failure
Tell the customer the charge failed and ask them to try again
Have the model decide whether to retry
Check the payment status first, or retry using the same idempotency key so the provider deduplicates
questions.explanation: Uncertain state on a non-idempotent action requires verification or idempotency keys to avoid double charges.
rationales: Possibly false, and risks a duplicate.
Model guessing about side effects is unsafe.

sources.title: Writing tools for agents — Anthropic Engineering
